title: Implied volatility
summary: Implied volatility is how much the market expects a stock to move, worked out backwards from the price of its options.
youtubeTitle: Implied volatility, explained with two stocks
body:
Let's say there are two stocks, A and B, and both of them trade at $100 today. If you look at how they got there, though, the two charts are very different, because A has moved along fairly calmly while B has been jumping up and down a lot more. In other words, B is much more **volatile**, which simply means that its price swings around more. Nobody knows where either stock will be next month, but the past gives you a hint of how bumpy the ride is likely to be.

## Where each stock might be in a month

If you look at where each stock could realistically end up a month from now, the two ranges are very different. For A, most of the likely outcomes are clustered tightly around $100. For B they're spread out much wider, so B could easily finish at $80 or at $120. Both ranges are centered on today's price, because nobody is saying that B is more likely to go up or down than A, only that it can wander a lot further in either direction.

## Why the option on the jumpier stock costs more

Now say you buy a call option on each of them. A call option is a contract that gives you the right to buy the stock at a fixed price, called the strike, and here the strike is $100 and the option runs for a month. In practice that means the call pays you whatever the stock ends up above $100 when the month is over, so if it ends at $107 you get $7, and if it ends at $100 or below you get nothing. That makes a call a bet that the stock goes up.

With A the payout will almost always be small, because A rarely gets far from $100. With B it's much more likely that the stock really gets far above $100. In this example B ends up above $120 about one time in six, which would pay you at least $20, while A practically never gets there.

You might ask why B's big drops don't cancel this out, since B is also much more likely to fall far. They don't, because the call pays nothing below $100 however low the stock goes, so a fall to $80 costs you no more than a fall to $99, and only the big rises make a difference. That's why the option on B is worth more, and in this example the call on B costs $8 while the call on A costs only $2.

## Working backwards from the price

**Implied volatility** works exactly the other way around. Instead of starting with how jumpy a stock is and working out what its option should cost, you start with the price the market is actually paying for the option, say $8, and ask how volatile the stock would have to be for that price to make sense. The answer is the implied volatility, and it's called "implied" because nobody states it directly and you have to read it off the price. For the $2 call on A it comes out at about 17 percent a year, and for the $8 call on B at about 70 percent.

The number is always given per year, so that options of different lengths can be compared with each other. Over a single month, 70 percent a year works out to a typical swing of about 20 percent, which is the $80 to $120 range from before, and 17 percent a year works out to about 5 percent, or around $5 either way for A.

## Before and after earnings

You can watch implied volatility move around a company's earnings, the day it reports its numbers for the past three months and usually holds an earnings call to talk about them. Before that day, implied volatility is high, because nobody knows the numbers yet. The stock could stay exactly where it is, but it could also jump five percent overnight, which on a regular day is much less likely, and people buying options have to pay for that chance of a jump, so option prices go up. Once the numbers are out, that unknown is gone, so the options get cheaper and implied volatility comes back down, because implied volatility is nothing more than the market's guess of how far the stock will move, read off the price of its options.

title: The Anthropic IPO and why everyone wants in
summary: Anthropic lost $104 billion in nine months, yet investors asked for six times the shares on offer in its IPO. Rapidly growing revenue explains the demand, though the valuation leaves little room for growth to slow.
youtubeTitle: Anthropic IPO - why everyone wants in, and what happens next
body:
On the evening of 18 November 2026, the banks running Anthropic's IPO were setting the price of its shares, and for every share on offer, investors had asked for about six. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, was selling 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 each, so investors wanted roughly five billion of them, from a company that had lost $104 billion in the first nine months of the year.

At $78 the sale itself comes to about $64 billion, which is less than the $75 billion SpaceX raised in June, the biggest IPO until now. But Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC also agreed to buy $26 billion of shares on the side at the same price, and with those it comes to around $90 billion, which would make it the biggest IPO ever. So why does everyone want a piece of a company that lost so much money?

## Sales grew twelvefold in a year

The main reason is how fast its revenue has grown. In the third quarter of 2025, Anthropic's sales were about $1.4 billion, and in the third quarter of 2026 they were about $17 billion, twelve times as much in a single year.

And most of that $104 billion loss is on paper. Early investors put money in through contracts that later convert into shares, and as Anthropic grew in value, those contracts became worth more. Accounting rules count that increase as a loss for the company even though no cash leaves it, and it makes up $94 billion of the $104 billion. Running the business itself lost only about $1.3 billion over those nine months.

## Slower growth and a steep valuation

That growth is already slowing down, though. In the second quarter of 2026 sales more than doubled in three months, whereas in the third quarter they grew by about half. If the third quarter had kept the second quarter's pace, it would have brought in about $28 billion instead of $17 billion.

The valuation hasn't slowed down with it. At $78 a share the whole company is valued at about $1.4 trillion, which is roughly twenty times its annual revenue at the latest quarter's pace. That means it would take twenty years of current sales, before paying a dollar of costs, just to match the price. On top of that, Anthropic has committed to almost $900 billion for chips and data centres, and those bills have to be paid whether growth keeps up or not.

## What usually happens on the first day

Demand like that usually pushes a stock up on its first day of trading, and the banks set it up that way on purpose. They price an IPO a bit below what the order book would bear, so that the institutional funds allocated shares get an immediate gain. With orders for six times as many shares as are available, most of those funds got fewer than they wanted, so they have to buy the rest on the open market, and that buying pushes the price up. The banks also cushion the price on the way down: they sell about 15 percent more shares than planned, and if the stock dips below the offer price in the first weeks, they buy those shares back in the market to support it.

Since 1980 the average American IPO has closed its first day about 19 percent higher. If Anthropic is priced at $78 and follows that pattern, it ends the day around $93, which is roughly what ordinary investors end up paying since most people can only buy once public trading starts.

## What happened after SpaceX went public

After the first day, it's a very different story. SpaceX was priced at $135 in June and closed its first day at about $161. Over the following months it traded as high as $226 and as low as $105, before closing at about $142 on 17 November. So the funds that got shares at the $135 offer price were still up about 5 percent, while anyone who bought at the end of the first day was down 12 percent.

The six-times demand for Anthropic is real, but the easy first-day gain mostly goes to the funds that get shares at the offer price. Anyone buying after that is betting that Anthropic can keep growing fast enough to justify a price of twenty times its annual sales.

title: Short selling
summary: Short selling means borrowing a share, selling it and buying it back later. You win if the price falls, but if it rises your losses have no limit.
youtubeTitle: Short selling, explained with one stock and $100
body:
Let's say there's a stock at $100 today, and you're pretty sure it's going to go down, maybe because the company has far too much debt, or because you think everybody is much too excited about it. If you owned the stock you could sell it, of course, but you don't own it, so how do you make money when a stock falls?

## How short selling works

You sell it anyway, and that's called **short selling**. You borrow one share from your broker, the company you buy and sell stocks through, which lends it to you out of the shares its other customers own, and you sell it right away for $100. Now you have the $100, but you owe somebody a share, and sooner or later you have to give it back. For as long as you keep the borrowed share, you pay a small fee, a bit like rent.

Say the stock drops to $70. Then you buy a share back for $70, give it back, and the $30 that's left over is yours. But if the stock climbs to $150, you still have to give back that share, and now it costs you $150, so you've lost $50.

## Why the losses have no limit

If you work this out for every price the stock could end up at, you can see why people are careful with this. When you own a stock, the most you can lose is the $100 you paid, because a price can't go below zero, and there's no limit on how much you can win. With a short it's exactly the other way around. The best thing that can happen is that the company goes bust and the stock drops to zero, and then you keep the whole $100. But if the stock goes to $200 you lose $100, at $300 you lose $200, and there's no limit to how far that goes, because there's no limit to how high a price can climb.

## What a short squeeze is

And it usually gets worse, because you're rarely the only one betting against the stock. While the price is going up, your broker wants to be sure you can still pay for the share you owe, so they ask you to put in more money, which is called a margin call. A lot of people give up at that point and buy the share back, but all that buying pushes the price up even further, so the next short seller loses even more and has to buy back too. When that happens to many short sellers one after the other, people call it a short squeeze.

## Volkswagen in October 2008

A famous short squeeze happened to Volkswagen in October 2008. Lots of hedge funds, investment funds that are free to bet on falling prices, had bet against the stock, so about 12 percent of all its shares had been sold short. Then on Sunday, 26 October, Porsche announced that it controlled about 74 percent of Volkswagen, and the German state of Lower Saxony held about another 20 percent. That left less than 6 percent of the shares that anyone could still buy, and the short sellers needed about twice that just to give back what they had borrowed.

On Friday, 24 October, the stock had closed at €210.85. On Monday it closed at €520, and on Tuesday it went above €1,000 during the day before closing at €945. For a moment Volkswagen was the most valuable listed company in the world, and the short sellers lost more than €20 billion. What drove the price that high was mostly the short sellers' own buying, because they had to buy back about twice as many shares as there were left to buy, and every one of them who gave up pushed the price higher for the ones still waiting.

title: Put options
summary: A put option is the right to sell a stock at a fixed price. If you own the stock it works like insurance, and if you don't it's a bet on a fall.
youtubeTitle: Put options, explained with one nervous stock owner
body:
Let's say you own a stock, and today it trades at $100. The company reports its numbers next month, and you're a bit nervous, because if the numbers disappoint, the stock could drop quite a lot. You could sell it now, but then if it goes up instead, you miss all of that. There's a way to keep the stock and still protect yourself against the drop, and that's to buy a put option.

## What a put option is

A **put option** gives you the right to sell a stock at a fixed price until a certain date. Let's say the fixed price, which is called the strike, is $95, and the put runs for three months, so at any time in those three months you can sell your stock for $95. You don't have to sell, because it's only a right, and of course that right isn't free: in this example the put costs $3. The person who sells you the put keeps those $3 whatever happens, and in return has to buy your stock for $95 if you ask, much like an insurance company that collects a premium and pays out when something goes wrong.

## What happens when the stock goes up or down

If the stock climbs to $120, you just forget about the put. The $3 you paid is gone, but your stock made $20, so you're still $17 ahead. If the stock falls to $80, though, you can still sell it for $95, so the put pays you $15, and that's exactly the case you were worried about.

If you work this out for every price the stock could end up at, you can see what the put really does. Without the put you just have the stock, and the lower it goes, the more you lose. With the put there's a floor, because however far the stock falls, you never end up with less than $92, which is the $95 you can sell for minus the $3 you paid. So a put works pretty much like insurance: you pay a small amount up front, most of the time you don't need it, but when things go really wrong, you're covered.

## A put without the stock is a bet on a fall

You don't even need to own the stock to buy a put, and then it's simply a bet that the stock goes down. You pay your $3, and if the stock ends up at $80, the put is worth $15, five times what you paid, because you could buy the stock for $80 and sell it straight away for $95. But if the stock stays above $95, nobody would use a right to sell at $95 when the market pays more, so the put is worth nothing and the $3 you paid is gone.

## Puts in the 2020 crash

You could see both of these in early 2020. The S&P 500, an index that tracks the stock prices of 500 of the biggest companies in the US, closed at 3,386 on 19 February and at 2,237 on 23 March, so it fell by about a third in just five weeks. People who held puts were covered, and some of them made a lot of money. But in those same weeks everybody wanted that kind of protection at once, so the people selling puts could ask far more for it, and anyone who only went looking for a put once the fall had started paid several times what it had cost a month earlier.

title: Leverage
summary: Leverage means investing with borrowed money. At five times leverage a 10% rise makes you 50%, but a 20% fall leaves you with nothing.
youtubeTitle: Leverage, explained with $10,000 and a loan
body:
Let's say you have $10,000, and there's a stock at $100 that you think is going to go up. You buy 100 shares with your money, and if the stock then rises 10 percent, to $110, your shares are worth $11,000, so you've made $1,000, which is also 10 percent. That's nice, but what if you could buy more shares than your own money allows?

## Buying with borrowed money

You can, because your broker, the firm that holds your account and buys the shares for you, will lend you money to buy more, and investing with borrowed money like that is called leverage. Let's say you borrow another $40,000, so you have $50,000 and can buy 500 shares. That's five times as many as your own money could buy, so we say you're five times leveraged. The loan isn't free, because you pay interest on it, but let's leave the interest out to keep the numbers simple.

Now the stock rises 10 percent again, to $110. Your 500 shares are worth $55,000, you pay back the $40,000, and you're left with $15,000. That's $5,000 more than you started with, so you've made 50 percent on a stock that only moved 10.

## The same loan works against you

Of course it works the other way too. If the stock falls 10 percent, to $90, your shares are worth $45,000, you still owe $40,000, and only $5,000 is left, so half your money is gone. If it falls to $80, the shares are worth exactly $40,000, the loan takes all of it, and you have nothing left, while without the loan you'd still have $8,000.

Across every possible stock price, the loan multiplies your result by five in both directions, and a drop of just 20 percent wipes you out completely. The reason is that your own $10,000 is only a fifth of the $50,000 in shares, and the broker wants its full $40,000 back whatever happens, so every dollar the shares lose comes out of your part. When the shares lose a fifth of their value, which is 20 percent, your part is gone.

And your broker won't even wait that long. They want their $40,000 back, so when the price gets close to that point, they ask you to put more money into the account, which is called a margin call, and if you don't have it, they sell your shares, right when they're cheapest.

## How leverage sank Long-Term Capital Management

That's how a hedge fund called Long-Term Capital Management, or LTCM, went under in 1998. A hedge fund is an investment fund for wealthy people and big institutions that can take much bigger risks than an ordinary fund, including borrowing a lot of money. Two of LTCM's partners, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, won the Nobel prize in economics in 1997, and in its first three years the fund returned 21, 43 and 41 percent after fees. At the start of 1998 it had about $4.7 billion of its own money and had borrowed more than $124.5 billion on top, so it held about $129 billion of investments, more than 25 times its own money.

At that level the same arithmetic leaves almost no room, because $4.72 billion is only about 3.7 percent of $129 billion, so a fall of less than 4 percent in what the fund owned was enough to wipe out all of its own money. In August 1998 Russia stopped paying on its bonds, which are loans that investors make to a government or a company in return for interest. Scared investors sold riskier bonds and rushed into the safest ones they could find, and that was the opposite of what LTCM had bet on, because the fund had bet that the difference between the safest bonds and riskier ones would shrink, and the rush made it grow instead.

In less than four months the fund lost $4.6 billion, almost all of the $4.7 billion it had started the year with. On 23 September 1998 the New York Fed, the New York branch of the US central bank, brought 14 banks and brokers together, and they put in $3.6 billion and took over 90 percent of the fund, because they were afraid its collapse would drag them down with it.

Borrowing makes every move bigger for you in both directions, and the more you borrow, the smaller the fall that takes away everything you put in.

title: Call options
summary: A call option gives you the right to buy a stock at a fixed price. Because calls are much cheaper than the stock itself, they amplify both your gains and the chance of losing everything you put in.
youtubeTitle: Call options, explained with one stock and $100
body:
Let's say there's a stock at $100 today, and you have a feeling it's going to go up over the next few months, maybe because the company is about to launch something new. The obvious thing would be to just buy the stock, but there's another way to bet on it, and that's to buy a call option.

## What a call option is

A **call option** is the right to buy a stock at a price you fix today, until a certain date. Let's say that price, which is called the strike, is $105, and the call runs for three months, so at any time in those three months you can buy the stock for $105. You don't have to use that right, but you do have to pay for it, and in this example it costs $3. The person who sells you the call keeps those $3 whatever happens, and in return has to sell you the stock for $105 if you ask.

## What happens when the stock goes up or down

Say the stock climbs to $125. Then you use your right, buy it for $105, and it's immediately worth $125, so your call is worth $20, and you only paid $3 for it. But if the stock drops to $90, well, nobody wants to pay $105 for something that costs $90 on the market, so the call is worth nothing and the $3 you paid is gone.

If you work this out for every price the stock could end up at, you can see how different the two bets are. With the stock, you win or lose dollar for dollar. With the call, you can never lose more than the $3, because below $105 the call is simply worth nothing, and above $105 it goes up just like the stock. You break even at $108, which is the $105 strike plus the $3 you paid, and above that you make money.

## Why calls are popular, and why that cuts both ways

Calls are popular mostly because they're so cheap compared to the stock, which gives you what's called leverage, meaning a small amount of money rides on a much bigger amount of stock. For the price of one share, $100, you can buy calls on 33 shares for $99. If the stock goes to $125, the one share is worth $125, but the 33 calls are worth $20 each, so $660 together. If the stock just stays at $100, though, the share is still worth $100, and the calls are worth nothing at all. The same happens if the stock rises a little, to $105, because the share has then made you $5 while the calls still run out worth nothing, so with calls you can be right about the direction and still lose everything you put in.

## GameStop in early 2021

Something like this happened with GameStop in January 2021. The stock closed at $19.95 on 12 January and at $347.51 on 27 January, so within about two weeks it went from around $20 to almost $350. These are prices from before July 2022, when GameStop split each share into four, so most charts today show them at a quarter of these numbers. A call that let you buy at $60 was worth almost nothing while the stock was at $20, but on 27 January it was worth nearly $300, because it let you buy for $60 a share that was selling for about $348. Three weeks later, on 19 February, the stock closed at $40.59, and the calls people had bought near the top were worth close to nothing, so the same leverage that had multiplied the money of those who bought early took nearly all of it from those who bought late.

title: Michael Burry's bet against housing
summary: In 2005 Michael Burry read the fine print of American mortgage bonds, bet against them, and in 2007 made his investors about $725 million.
youtubeTitle: How Michael Burry bet against the housing market
body:
In 2005, house prices in America had been going up every year for as long as anyone could remember. Banks were lending money to almost anybody who wanted to buy a home, and hardly anyone thought that could go wrong. Michael Burry, a former doctor in California, thought it could. He had quit his neurology residency at Stanford to run a small investment fund of his own, Scion Capital, and he did something with the bonds behind all this lending that almost nobody bothered to do, which was to read the fine print.

## What was inside the mortgage bonds

The banks that made home loans mostly didn't keep them. They bundled thousands of loans into a bond and sold it, so whoever owned the bond got the monthly payments from all those homeowners, and if the homeowners stopped paying, it was the bond owner who lost money and not the bank that had made the loans. When Burry read what was inside these bonds, he found loans to people who never had to show their income, and lots of loans with a teaser rate.

A teaser rate is a low interest rate that only lasts for the first couple of years. Say you borrow $200,000 for 30 years at 7 percent, so you pay about $1,330 a month. After two years the rate jumps to 11 percent, and now the same loan costs you about $1,880 a month. Lots of people couldn't pay that, so Burry figured that when these loans reset in 2007, a lot of homeowners would simply stop paying, and the bonds that lived on their payments would be worth far less than their owners believed.

## Insurance on bonds he didn't own

So he wanted to bet against those bonds, and the way to do that was a kind of insurance called a credit default swap, which you can buy even if you don't own the bonds. If you insure $10 million of them, you pay a fee every year, something like $250,000, and as long as the bonds keep paying, that money is gone. But if the homeowners stop paying and the bonds become worthless, you get the whole $10 million, which is forty times what you paid in a year.

Burry bought his first ones from Deutsche Bank in May 2005, ten million dollars on each of six bonds, and he kept going. By October he had insured at least a billion dollars of mortgage bonds, and he had to keep paying the fees on all of it for as long as the homeowners kept paying.

## Two years of waiting

But then nothing happened. House prices kept going up, the homeowners kept paying, and Burry kept paying his fees, so on the $10 million in the example, two years of waiting would have cost half a million dollars with nothing to show for it. In 2006 Scion lost about 18 percent while the stock market went up about 16, which meant his investors would have done far better by just buying the market, and they were furious.

A lot of them wanted their money back. Burry still believed the loans would go bad once the teaser rates ran out, so he used a clause in the fund's contract to move the swaps into a side pocket, a separate part of the fund that investors couldn't take their money out of. That locked their money into his bet, and it made them even angrier.

## When the teaser rates ran out

And then, in 2007, the teaser rates ran out. People who couldn't afford the higher payments stopped paying, so less and less money flowed into the bonds, and the bonds fell apart, because a bond is only worth the payments that come into it. That was exactly what Burry's insurance paid out on, so the swaps he had been paying fees on for two years were suddenly worth a fortune, and he sold them back to the banks at a large profit.

He made his investors about $725 million, including the ones whose money he had locked in, and he made about $100 million for himself. In 2008 he closed the fund. The loans that sank those bonds had been described in the fine print all along, and what made Burry rich was that he read it and then held on through two years of fees and furious investors until the homeowners stopped paying.

title: How much can you lose short selling?
summary: In theory short selling carries unlimited losses. In practice your broker, a stop order or a call option caps the loss, though only the call holds when a stock jumps overnight.
youtubeTitle: Can you really lose an infinite amount by short selling?
body:
Short selling is a way to bet that a stock will fall. Let's say a stock trades at $100, so you borrow one share from your broker (the firm that holds your account and trades for you), sell it straight away for $100, and promise to buy a share back later and return it. If the price falls, you buy it back for less than you sold it for and keep the difference, but if it rises, you have to pay more than you got, and that difference is your loss.

The lower the stock goes, the more you make, up to $100 if it falls all the way to zero. The higher it goes, though, the more you lose, and because there is no ceiling on how high a stock price can climb, there is no theoretical limit to how much you can lose. That's why people say that with short selling you can lose an infinite amount of money, and in theory, that's true.

## Your broker stops the loss, but at the worst moment

In practice your losses do stop somewhere, because you don't have infinite money and your broker knows it. While the price climbs, the broker keeps checking that your account can still pay for the share you owe, and when it can't, they buy the share back for you, whether you like it or not. That isn't really protection, though, because they buy when the price is already high and your loss is already big, and if the price jumps far enough in one go, buying the share back costs more than everything in your account, so you end up owing the broker the rest.

## A stop order works until the price jumps

So most people set their own limit with a stop order, an instruction you give the broker in advance: if the stock ever trades at $120, buy the share back right away. If the price climbs slowly, that works nicely: it passes $120, your share is bought back, and you've lost $20 and not a cent more.

But the $120 is only a trigger, and once the stock reaches it, the order buys at whatever price it can get. Let's say the stock closes at $100 in the evening, and overnight the company announces that someone wants to buy it. Everyone who owns the stock now expects that buyer to pay more for it, so nobody wants to sell at $100 anymore, and the next morning it opens at $150. Your stop never had a chance to buy at $120, because the price was never there, so it buys at $150 and you've lost $50 instead of $20.

## A call option is the only real cap

The one thing that really caps the loss is a call option, a contract that gives you the right, but not the duty, to buy a share at a price you fix today, at any time until the contract runs out. Let's say you buy a call that lets you buy the share at $120 at any time in the next three months, and it costs you $2. Now it doesn't matter how far the stock jumps, because you can always get the share for $120 and hand it back to the lender.

Take the overnight jump to $150 again. Buying back the share costs you $50 more than you sold it for, but your right to buy at $120 saves you $30, and you paid $2, so you've lost $22. At any price above $120 you end up with the same $22, which is the $20 between $100 and $120 plus the $2 you paid. And if the stock just falls like you hoped, you never use the call and the $2 is simply gone, a bit like insurance you didn't need.

## The KaloBios short in 2015

A trader called Joe Campbell found this out the hard way in November 2015. He had about $37,000 in his account at E*Trade, and he was short a small drug company called KaloBios, which closed at $2.07 on Wednesday, 18 November. That evening the news came out that a group of investors led by Martin Shkreli had taken a majority stake, so they now owned most of the company, and overnight the stock rose as much as 1,000 percent. His shares were bought back at about $16 to $18.50 each (reports differ), so his $37,000 was gone, and on top of that he owed E*Trade $106,445.56, which makes a loss of about $143,000 on a stock that had closed at about two dollars.

So a short can't really lose an infinite amount, but it can lose far more than everything you have, and when the price jumps overnight, the only limit that holds is one you paid for in advance.

title: How Bill Hwang and Archegos lost $36 billion
summary: Bill Hwang turned $1.5 billion into $36 billion in a year with borrowed money and hidden swaps, then lost all of it within days in March 2021.
youtubeTitle: Archegos - how Bill Hwang lost $36 billion in days
body:
In March 2021 a man called Bill Hwang had bets on stocks worth about $160 billion, and more than $120 billion of that was really the banks' money. Each of those banks knew about its own part of his bets, but none of them knew how big the whole thing was, and when it came apart, all of Hwang's own money was gone within days and the banks went on to lose more than $10 billion between them.

Hwang's firm, Archegos, didn't manage anyone else's money, only his own family's. In March 2020 it had about $1.5 billion, and one year later it had $36 billion, twenty-four times as much in a single year. He did that mostly with leverage, which means betting with borrowed money on top of your own.

## How borrowed money multiplied everything

With $160 billion of bets and only $36 billion of his own, every move in those stocks hit his own money more than four times as hard. If his stocks rose 10 percent, he made $16 billion, which was 44 percent of everything he had, and that is how a fortune can grow so fast. But it works the same way down, because every loss comes out of his own money first while the banks still want all of theirs back, so if the stocks fell by just 22.5 percent, the whole $36 billion would be gone.

## Bets nobody could see

The strange thing is that nobody knew, because Hwang didn't buy most of those shares himself. He had the banks buy them and signed a contract with each one, called a total return swap, that gave him every gain and every loss on those shares as if he owned them. The shares sat in the banks' names, so he never had to report them publicly, and because he spread his bets over many banks, at least nine according to US prosecutors, each bank only saw its own part. For some companies his bets added up to more than half of all their shares, and none of the banks knew.

## How ViacomCBS brought it down

One of his biggest bets was ViacomCBS, and partly because he kept buying more of it, its stock went from about $37 at the start of 2021 to just over $100 on Monday, 22 March. That evening the company announced that it would sell new shares to raise $3 billion, which meant a lot more shares looking for buyers. The stock fell 9 percent the next day, and when the new shares were priced at $85, it fell another 23 percent.

For Hwang that was a disaster. When you bet with a bank's money, the bank keeps some of your own money as a cushion, and when your stocks fall, it makes what's called a margin call, which means it calls you and asks you to top that cushion up. Archegos couldn't pay, so on Thursday it told the banks, which talked about selling his shares slowly and together so the price wouldn't crash. But nobody wanted to be the last one still holding them, because every bank that sold would push the price down for the next, and once Hwang's money was used up, every further fall would come out of the bank's own pocket.

So on Friday, 26 March, Goldman Sachs sold about $10.5 billion of his shares in huge blocks and Morgan Stanley about $8 billion, and ViacomCBS fell another 27 percent that day, to $48, which was less than half of what it had been on Monday. Within days Hwang's $36 billion was gone, and Goldman got out almost without a loss.

## Who paid

The banks that waited had to sell into a falling market. Credit Suisse lost $5.5 billion and Nomura almost $3 billion, UBS lost about $900 million, and Morgan Stanley, even though it had sold on Friday, also lost about $900 million, so the banks lost more than $10 billion in total. Two years later, after more losses and scandals, Credit Suisse was taken over by UBS.

In July 2024 Hwang was convicted on ten of eleven counts, including fraud and market manipulation. The fraud was that he had lied to the banks about how big and how concentrated his bets were, and in November 2024 he was sentenced to 18 years in prison. The borrowed money that turned $1.5 billion into $36 billion in a year worked just as hard on the way down, and because the bets were hidden across so many banks, none of them could see how far it could fall until it was already falling.

title: The dot-com bubble and how it burst
summary: $10,000 in the Nasdaq in 1995 grew to about $50,000 by March 2000. Then the dot-com bubble burst and the index fell 78 percent in two and a half years.
youtubeTitle: The dot-com bubble, explained with $10,000
body:
In the summer of 1995 you could have put $10,000 into the Nasdaq, the American stock index that's full of tech companies. Three years later your money would have doubled, by the end of 1999 it would have been above $40,000, and in March 2000 it would have reached about $50,000, five times as much in less than five years. But if you had put your $10,000 in at that moment in March 2000 instead, two and a half years later you would have had about $2,200 left.

## Why investors wanted every internet company

The internet had arrived, and suddenly you could buy a book or a plane ticket from your living room. Investors could see that this was going to change everything, so they wanted a piece of every company that had something to do with it, even though many of those had never made a single dollar of profit. That didn't seem to matter, because people looked at how fast a company was growing and how many visitors its website had, and much less at whether it earned any money.

So lots of young companies went public, selling their shares on the stock market for the first time, and the shares often shot up on the very first day. In December 1999 a company called VA Linux sold its shares at $30, and by the end of that day they were trading at $239, almost eight times as much, for a company that was losing money. The people paying $239 couldn't have been counting on VA Linux's profits, because it had none, so they were counting on someone else paying even more later, and when prices go up mostly because people expect them to keep going up, we call it a bubble.

## Why the market turned in March 2000

In March 2000 the mood shifted. The Fed had been raising interest rates since the summer of 1999, so money was getting more expensive to borrow, which is hardest on companies that don't make a profit and keep needing new money from investors and lenders. That same month the magazine Barron's looked at 207 internet companies and worked out that 51 of them, about one in four, would run out of cash within a year.

So investors started asking the question they had skipped, which is when a company is actually going to make money, and for a lot of them there was no good answer. People who had bought because they expected prices to keep rising had no reason left to hold on, so they sold, and with fewer and fewer buyers willing to pay the old prices, the prices kept dropping.

## A two-and-a-half-year crash

The Nasdaq kept falling for two and a half years, until in October 2002 it was 78 percent below the top. Your $10,000 from 1995 would have been back down to about $11,000, so seven years after putting it in, you would have been only about $1,000 ahead. The $10,000 put in at the peak was down to about $2,200, and the Nasdaq only got back above its 2000 peak in April 2015, fifteen years later.

## Amazon survived, Pets.com didn't

The people who said the internet would change everything weren't wrong. Amazon's shares fell about 94 percent, from about $107 in December 1999 to about $6 in September 2001, and today Amazon is one of the biggest companies in the world. Most of the others didn't survive, though.

The best-known of them is Pets.com, which sold pet food and supplies online. In January 2000 it paid over a million dollars for a Super Bowl ad with a sock puppet dog, in February it went public at $11 a share, and only nine months later, in November, it announced it was closing down, with its shares at 19 cents. Part of the problem was that it often sold things for less than it paid for them, so every extra sale added to its losses, and heavy bags of dog food are expensive to ship.

People who bought in 2000 were right that the internet would change everything, and those who bought near the top still lost most of their money, because they had paid for that future in almost every internet company at once and only a few of those companies lived long enough to see it.

title: The Enron scandal and how the fraud worked
summary: Enron booked projected future profits on day one, hid its losses in side companies propped up by its own stock, and fell from $90 a share to 26 cents in fifteen months.
youtubeTitle: The Enron fraud, explained
body:
In 2000 Enron was the hottest company in America. Its revenue had gone from $13 billion to more than $100 billion in just four years, Fortune magazine kept calling it the most innovative company in the country, and its share price had more than tripled, to $90. And its own employees had a lot riding on it, because more than half of the money in their retirement plan was in Enron stock. Fifteen months after that $90 record, the shares were worth 26 cents.

Wall Street was so hungry for Enron that in January 2000, when the company just told analysts it would start trading internet capacity the way it traded gas, the stock jumped by about a quarter in a single day.

## Booking profits from a deal that never happened

That summer Enron signed a twenty-year deal with Blockbuster to stream films to people's homes. The deal never got past a test in four cities and was called off in March 2001, but Enron booked more than $110 million of profit from it. It could do that because of an accounting method called mark-to-market, which Jeffrey Skilling, who later ran the company, had pushed for, and which the SEC had approved for Enron back in 1992. Mark-to-market let Enron estimate what a deal would earn over all twenty years and count that entire projection as profit on the day the contract was signed.

So a big part of the profit Wall Street loved was money Enron had never received, and from the Blockbuster deal it never would, because the venture never brought in any real revenue.

## Where the losses went

When a deal went bad, that projected profit had to turn into a loss, and every loss Enron showed would have eaten into the earnings that kept its stock price up. So the finance chief, Andrew Fastow, hid them. He built a maze of side companies, with names like Chewco, LJM and the Raptors, to keep the losses, along with billions of dollars of debt, off Enron's books, and he ran some of those companies himself and pocketed more than $30 million from them.

But these side companies were backed by Enron's own shares, so they could only carry the losses as long as the share price kept rising, and if it fell, the losses would land back on Enron just when its stock was already falling.

## How it fell apart in 2001

In 2001 the price started to slide, and in August Skilling, who had been chief executive for only six months, suddenly quit. In September, with the stock at about $27, the chairman, Ken Lay, told employees in an online chat that it was "an incredible bargain", and he didn't mention that he had been selling his own shares.

With the stock still falling, the side companies couldn't carry the losses anymore, so in October they came back onto Enron's books and Enron reported a loss of $618 million for the quarter. In November it admitted that it had overstated its profits ever since 1997. Now investors couldn't trust any of the profits they had paid for, so they sold, and less than a month later, on 2 December 2001, Enron went bankrupt, the biggest bankruptcy America had seen until then. The shares that had been worth $90 were worth 26 cents.

## Who paid for it

With more than half of their retirement plan in Enron stock, thousands of employees lost their jobs and their savings at once. Skilling and Lay were both convicted of fraud in 2006. Fastow, who had pleaded guilty, got six years in prison, Skilling got twenty-four, later cut to fourteen, and Lay died before he could be sentenced.

A big part of what made Enron look so successful was projected profit and hidden losses, and the people who paid for it in the end were the ones who had trusted its numbers, above all its own employees.

title: How Credit Suisse disappeared in one weekend
summary: Credit Suisse was over 160 years old and came through 2008 without state money, yet in March 2023 a bank run finished it in a single weekend.
youtubeTitle: How Credit Suisse disappeared in a single weekend
body:
On Sunday evening, 19 March 2023, Credit Suisse, a bank founded in 1856 and one of Switzerland's two big banks, was sold to its rival UBS for three billion francs. In 2007 the same bank had been worth about a hundred billion. The Swiss government pushed the deal through over the weekend under emergency law, so the shareholders who owned Credit Suisse were never even asked.

The strange part is that Credit Suisse was supposed to be one of the safe ones. In 2008, when UBS had to be rescued with money from the Swiss state, Credit Suisse raised about ten billion francs from private investors instead. And after 2008 the rules got much stricter, so the big Swiss banks had to hold far more of their own money, called capital, as a cushion against losses. So how does a bank like that disappear in a single weekend?

## What a bank does with your money

The answer is a bank run, and it's so dangerous because a bank doesn't keep your money in a vault. It lends most of it out, often for years, so at any moment it can only pay back a small part of what its clients have deposited. If too many of them want their money back at once, the bank has to sell what it owns in a hurry, for far less than it's worth, and the moment it can't pay a client back, it has defaulted and it's finished, even if every loan it made was perfectly fine.

The bigger capital cushion doesn't help against that, because capital is the money that comes from a bank's owners rather than its clients, and it gets lent out like the rest. It takes the losses when loans go bad, but it can't turn a mortgage that runs for years into cash a client can take out today, so a bank lives on its clients trusting it enough to leave their money where it is.

## How Credit Suisse lost that trust

Credit Suisse kept giving its clients reasons to doubt it. In 2019 it came out that the bank had hired private detectives to follow Iqbal Khan, one of its own former managers, who had left for UBS, and a few months later the chief executive, Tidjane Thiam, had to go.

Then in March 2021 it was hit twice within a few weeks. First it had to freeze about ten billion dollars of its clients' money tied to a lender called Greensill, which went bust a week later, and then it lost about five and a half billion dollars of its own money on an investment firm called Archegos, so now its clients really began to wonder whether their money was still safe there.

In early October 2022, rumours spread online that a major international bank was about to fail, and everyone thought of Credit Suisse. In the last three months of that year its clients took out about 110 billion francs, and the bank only just held on by raising four billion francs of new capital and selling off part of its business.

## The last week

On 10 March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in America, and investors everywhere went looking for the next weak bank. Five days later, Ammar Al Khudairy, chairman of Credit Suisse's biggest shareholder, the Saudi National Bank, was asked on Bloomberg TV whether his bank would put in more money, and he said "absolutely not". Investors feared Credit Suisse could now fail, and since shareholders are last in line when a bank fails and usually end up with nothing, they sold, and the shares fell by almost a quarter that day. Clients ran for the same reason: on the Monday they had taken out 1.6 billion francs, and on that Wednesday alone they took out 13.2 billion.

The next day the Swiss National Bank lent Credit Suisse about 48 billion francs to pay the clients who wanted out, but a loan doesn't bring back trust, and clients kept taking out more than ten billion francs a day. By the weekend the regulators concluded that the bank couldn't open on Monday, and a bank that can't open can't pay its clients, which is the default the run had been heading for. So the government pushed UBS to take it over, and the deal was announced on Sunday evening.

## Who paid and who won

The shareholders paid, since their bank went for about three percent of what it had been worth in 2007. UBS won, and a few months later it reported a profit of 29 billion dollars for a single quarter, 28.9 billion of which came from paying far less for Credit Suisse than its assets minus its debts were worth, a gap that accounting rules let a buyer book as profit.

After 2008 the rules made Credit Suisse hold a much bigger cushion against losses, but no cushion keeps a bank open once its clients stop trusting it and all want their money back at the same time.

title: Why the Great Depression lasted so long
summary: How a 1929 stock crash, debts that got heavier as prices fell, and thousands of bank runs kept America down for more than ten years.
youtubeTitle: Why the Great Depression lasted ten years
body:
On 27 April 1933, in Le Mars, Iowa, a crowd of farmers dragged Judge Charles Bradley out of his courtroom, put a rope around his neck and demanded that he stop signing foreclosures, the court orders that let a lender take a farm when its owner can't pay back the loan. Bradley still refused, and martial law followed. Most of those farmers had never owned a single share, and yet what had brought them there was the crash on Wall Street three and a half years earlier, which kept America down for more than ten years. So how does a stock market crash do that?

It started with fear. In less than a month, from mid-October to mid-November 1929, the Dow Jones lost more than 40 percent, and when people don't know what's coming, they put off the big things, like a new car or a new radio. So factories sold less and laid off workers, and those workers stopped buying too. In 1929 about one worker in thirty had no job, and by 1933 it was one in four.

## The more they paid, the more they owed

Lots of Americans were in debt, farmers most of all, and a loan is a fixed number of dollars. But with less money going around, crop prices fell, and by 1932 farmers got less than half of what they had got in 1929, so to pay back the same loan they had to sell more than twice as much. And since every farmer in debt was doing the same, they all brought more to market at once, which pushed prices down even further.

The economist Irving Fisher, who had lost a fortune in the crash himself, called this loop debt deflation, and he put it in one line: "the more the debtors pay, the more they owe." By his count, Americans had paid back about a fifth of their debts by March 1933, but since every dollar now bought so much more, what they still owed weighed about 40 percent more than before. For a farmer, that meant the harder he worked to pay off his loan, the heavier the rest of it got, until the lender went to court to take the farm and a judge signed the order.

## The banks went down too

All those unpaid loans dragged the banks down with them. Nothing was insured back then, so as soon as people heard their bank was in trouble, they ran to get their money out, and since a bank lends most deposits out, it could pay only the first in line before it had to close. About 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933, and because most money sat in bank accounts, about a third of all the money in the country disappeared with them. With a third less money going around, prices fell even faster, and every debt got heavier again.

The Federal Reserve could have created new money to stop this, but it cared more about keeping every dollar swappable for gold. So in October 1931, after Britain had left the gold standard, the Fed raised its interest rate from 1.5 to 3.5 percent, which made it more worthwhile to hold dollars than to swap them for gold, but also made every loan more expensive in the middle of the collapse.

## How Roosevelt broke the loop

For three and a half years nobody broke the loop, until Franklin Roosevelt became president on 4 March 1933 and broke it in two places. First he closed every bank in the country for about a week, and that June Congress passed deposit insurance, so that if a bank failed, the government would pay its depositors back and nobody needed to run anymore. Then he cut the dollar loose from gold, so the money supply could grow without gold behind every dollar, and prices rose again. Now the loop ran backwards: debts got lighter, people started buying, factories hired again, and by 1937 unemployment was down to about one in seven.

## Why it came back in 1937

But then Washington decided the patient was cured. The government cut its spending, new payroll taxes started taking money out of workers' pay, and the Fed doubled the share of their deposits that banks had to hold back instead of lending out. Within a year unemployment jumped back up to 19 percent. In the end it took the Second World War, with factories building ships and planes day and night, to get America back to work, and by 1944 only about one worker in a hundred had no job.

The farmers in Le Mars never owned a share, but the crash set off a loop in which falling prices made every debt heavier and failing banks made money scarcer, and because nobody broke it for three and a half years and Washington set it going again in 1937, farmers and workers like them paid for that crash for more than ten years.

title: Bulls and bears
summary: A bull market rises and a bear market falls. The words come from 1700s London and an old saying about selling a bear's skin before you catch the bear.
youtubeTitle: Why a bull and a bear? Where the stock market words come from
body:
You've probably heard that a rising stock market is called a bull market and a falling one a bear market, and that people who bet on rising prices are called bulls, while the ones who bet on falling prices are called bears. But where do those two words come from? The explanation you'll hear most often is easy to remember, but it's wrong.

## Horns up, claws down

The usual story is about how the two animals fight. A bull attacks by throwing its horns up, and a bear attacks by striking down with its claws, so the bull stands for prices going up and the bear for prices going down. It's a good picture to remember them by, and you can keep using it for that, but it isn't where the words came from.

## Selling the bear's skin

The words come from London in the early 1700s, and from an old saying that was already around in the 1500s: don't sell the bear's skin before you've caught the bear. A hunter who sells the skin first has promised something he doesn't have yet, and he has to hope the hunt goes his way.

Some traders in London did exactly that with shares. They agreed to sell shares they didn't own yet, to be handed over at a later date, and hoped the price would fall before then, so they could buy the shares cheaper and keep the difference. By about 1705 "bearskin" was being used for deals like these, and in 1709 the London magazine *The Tatler* was already calling the traders themselves bears. Today we would call a bet like that short selling. So the bear in "bear market" was never about how a bear fights, because the link to the stock market came from the saying about its skin.

## Where the bull comes in

The bull came along a few years later. Depending on which source you trust, it was first recorded in 1714 or in 1718, and it was most likely picked simply because it starts with the same sound and sounded good next to the bear. By 1718 the pair had made it onto the London stage: Susanna Centlivre's play *A Bold Stroke for a Wife* opened in London on 3 February 1718, and in a scene set in Jonathan's Coffee-house in Change Alley, one trader asks another, "Are you a Bull or a Bear to-day, Abraham?"

So the horns and the claws are a fine way to remember which is which, but the bear was named after traders who sold what they didn't have yet, and the bull most likely got its place next to it only because the two words sounded good together.

title: The rise and fall of General Electric
summary: In 2000 GE was the most valuable company on earth. Then its lending arm nearly sank it, and by 2018 its shares had fallen under $7 for the second time.
youtubeTitle: The rise and fall of GE
body:
On 28 August 2000, General Electric's shares closed at 60 dollars, and GE was worth about 594 billion dollars, more than any other company on earth. It went all the way back to Thomas Edison and his light bulb, and in 1896 it was one of the twelve companies in the very first Dow Jones Industrial Average, the famous index of big American companies. By 2000 it made jet engines, power plants and MRI scanners, and it owned the TV network NBC. It was what Nvidia or Apple are today, a giant that nobody could imagine ever falling from the top. Yet by March 2009 its shares were under seven dollars, and after they climbed back, they fell under seven again. So how does a company like that fall, and fall twice?

## How GE got so big

From 1981 to 2001 GE was run by Jack Welch, and Wall Street loved how fast it kept growing under him, so the share price went up more than 40 times, from 1.40 dollars (adjusted for later share splits) to 60, and in 1999 Fortune magazine named him Manager of the Century.

But a big part of that growth had nothing to do with machines. Back in 1932, in the Great Depression, GE had started lending families money so they could buy its fridges and other appliances on credit, and over the decades that lending arm, GE Capital, grew into one of the biggest lenders in America, with credit cards, mortgages and whole fleets of airplanes that it leased out. If GE Capital had been a bank, it would have been one of the biggest banks in the country, and by the mid-2000s about half of GE's profits came from lending money instead of from anything it built.

## Why a lender can fall so fast

A lender lives on borrowed money, and the way GE Capital borrowed made it fragile. It borrowed for weeks or months at a time and lent for years, so every time one of its short loans came due, it had to borrow again to pay it back. That works as long as the people lending to you trust you. But in 2008, when big banks started to fail, the people GE Capital borrowed from got scared, even of GE, and stopped lending. A lender that can't borrow can't pay back its old loans when they come due, and the moment it misses a payment, it has defaulted.

So GE had to ask Warren Buffett for money, and in October 2008 his company Berkshire Hathaway put in three billion dollars. A month later the US government agreed to guarantee GE Capital's debts. Investors saw a company that needed rescuing and feared that even GE could go bust, and since shareholders are last in line when a company goes under and usually end up with nothing, they sold. By March 2009 the share price had fallen from 60 dollars to 6.66, a drop of almost 90 percent.

## The second fall

GE survived, and by 2016 its shares had climbed back to more than 30 dollars. But in late 2015 GE had made one more big bet, paying about ten billion dollars for a power-plant business just before demand for new gas turbines collapsed. A business that sells power plants earns little when nobody is ordering them, so what GE had just paid for was suddenly worth far less, and investors who had held GE as a safe giant sold again.

In June 2018 GE was thrown out of the Dow Jones after 111 years in a row. That October it admitted on its books that its power business was worth 23 billion dollars less than it had said, and by December the shares were back under seven dollars. In the end Edison's old company split itself into three: GE HealthCare was spun off in 2023, GE Vernova in 2024, and what was left, GE Aerospace, kept the old name.

## Today's giants

GE wasn't the only giant of 2000 that lost its place. Of the ten most valuable American companies at the end of 2000, only Microsoft was still in the top ten in November 2026. The others, like Cisco and Intel, were passed by Nvidia, Apple and the rest of what people now call the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Tesla. Since an index fund buys every company in proportion to its size, about a third of the money in an S&P 500 index fund now sits in those seven, and just like GE in 2000, nobody can imagine them falling.

In 2000 GE looked as safe as any company on earth, and nine of the ten biggest American companies of that year have since dropped out of the top ten, so it would be no surprise if some of today's giants end up much smaller one day too.

title: How Keith Gill turned $53,000 into $580 million
summary: Keith Gill bet $53,000 on GameStop with cheap call options, caught hedge funds in a short squeeze, and later showed an account worth over $580 million.
youtubeTitle: How Keith Gill turned $53,000 into $580 million on GameStop
body:
In 2019, Wall Street was sure that GameStop, the chain of video-game shops, was headed for bankruptcy, because gamers were downloading games instead of buying discs, and the stock had fallen to about five dollars. Big hedge funds were betting that it would fall further. On the other side was Keith Gill, who worked at an insurance company in Massachusetts and was about to bet 53,000 dollars of his savings that they were wrong, and less than two years later the biggest of those funds needed a rescue.

## How the hedge funds bet against GameStop

The hedge funds shorted GameStop, which means they borrowed shares, sold them straight away, and planned to buy them back later for pennies, return them and keep the difference. A borrowed share that gets sold ends up with a new buyer, whose broker can lend it out to be shorted again, so by January 2021 about 140 percent of all the GameStop shares available to trade had been sold short. That is dangerous, because a short seller can make at most what he sold the shares for, but if the price rises his losses have no limit, since he still has to buy the shares back at whatever they cost.

## Gill's bet

Gill read GameStop's numbers in his basement and disagreed. The company still had plenty of cash and new consoles were on the way, so he didn't think it was going bust any time soon, and in September 2019 he put 53,000 dollars on it.

At five dollars a share, that money would have bought about 10,000 shares. Instead Gill bought call options, contracts that gave him the right to buy 100,000 shares at eight dollars each until mid-January 2021. Because almost nobody thought GameStop would get to eight dollars, that right cost him only about 54 cents a share. If the stock stayed below eight dollars, his money would be gone, but when the options ran out, every dollar the stock stood above eight would be worth 100,000 dollars to him, ten times what plain shares would have made.

Every month he posted a screenshot of his account on Reddit's WallStreetBets forum as DeepFuckingValue and streamed on YouTube in a red headband as Roaring Kitty, and for a year people laughed at him. Then in late 2020 Ryan Cohen, a billionaire who had co-founded Chewy, bought into GameStop, and the stock climbed past eight dollars, then past twenty. Thousands of Reddit traders saw that Gill had been right and piled in, and every share they bought pushed the price higher against the hedge funds.

## The short squeeze

When you short a stock at five dollars and it climbs to forty, you're down 35 dollars on every share, and your broker forces you to buy the shares back right away, before your losses grow bigger than the money you have. Because the hedge funds had shorted more shares than were available to trade, they all had to buy at once, and their buying drove the price even higher, which forced still more short sellers to buy, in a chain reaction called a short squeeze.

On 28 January 2021 GameStop hit 483 dollars a share. Short sellers lost more than six billion dollars that month, and the biggest of them, Melvin Capital, lost more than half its money in January alone, needed a rescue from two other big funds, and shut down in May 2022. The day before the peak, Gill's account was worth almost 48 million dollars, and as his January options were about to run out, he sold enough of them to lock in more than 13 million in cash and kept the rest of his bet in GameStop.

On the day of the peak, Robinhood and other trading apps stopped their customers from buying GameStop, because of the deposits demanded from them by the clearinghouse that settles their trades. Their customers could only sell, the price crashed, and by February GameStop was back around 40 dollars, so the people who had bought near the top lost most of their money.

## What Gill did next

On 18 February 2021 Gill was called before Congress alongside the billionaire fund bosses, and from his basement he told the lawmakers, "I like the stock." The next day he used part of his cash to double his shares, buying 50,000 more at about 40 dollars, and in April he used his remaining options to buy another 50,000, for 200,000 in all. Then he went quiet, until June 2024, when he came back and showed his account one last time: 5 million GameStop shares and 120,000 call options, worth about 586 million dollars on 6 June.

The hedge funds had sold short more GameStop shares than there were to buy back, so once the price turned they all had to buy at the same time, and that rush made a bet people had laughed at worth a fortune and shut Melvin Capital down.

title: Shiller P/E ratio (CAPE)
summary: The Shiller P/E compares a price with ten years of inflation-adjusted profit, so one bad or great year can't make stocks look cheap or expensive.
youtubeTitle: The Shiller P/E ratio (CAPE), explained
body:
When you look at a stock, the share price alone doesn't tell you whether it's cheap or expensive, because what you're paying for is a slice of the company's profits. The usual measure is the price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, which divides the share price by what the company earned per share over the last year, meaning its profit divided by the number of shares. If a stock trades at $100 and the company earned $5 per share, its P/E is 20, so you're paying twenty times one year's profit.

## How one bad year fools the regular P/E

That works fine in a steady year, but profits swing between booms and recessions, and that's where a one-year P/E plays a trick on you. Suppose a recession hits, worried investors sell, and the stock falls by half, to $50, even though the business itself is fine. If its profit drops for that one year from $5 a share to $1, the P/E is now $50 divided by $1, which is 50, so the stock looks two and a half times as expensive as before at exactly the moment it costs half as much.

## Ten years of profit instead of one

To fix that, the economist Robert Shiller, who later won the Nobel prize in economics in 2013, replaced one year of profit with the average profit of the last ten years, adjusted for inflation. Adjusting for inflation means that older profits are converted into today's money, so a dollar earned ten years ago counts for what it would buy today. Shiller worked out the idea with John Campbell in a paper published in 1988, and the result is called the Shiller P/E, or the CAPE ratio, short for cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings, because a ten-year window smooths out the booms and recessions.

Over the full ten years, counting the good years and the bad one together, our company still averaged $5 a share. So at $50 the Shiller P/E is 50 divided by 5, which is 10, and that shows the stock really is half as expensive as it was at 20.

## What it showed in 2009 and in 2000

The same thing happened to the S&P 500, an index of 500 big American companies, during the financial crisis. Between October 2007 and March 2009 its price fell 57 percent, and huge losses at banks and other companies pushed the profits of the past twelve months down by 92 percent from their 2007 level. Because profits fell much further than prices, the regular P/E went above 120 in May 2009 and made stocks look wildly overpriced right around the bottom. The Shiller P/E, though, fell to about 13 in March 2009, well below its average since 1881 of about 17, and over the next ten years the index more than tripled.

In a boom it works the other way, and it shows when prices have run far ahead of what companies steadily earn. At the top of the dot-com bubble, around the turn of 2000, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E hit a record of about 44. In March 2000, the same month the index peaked, Shiller published his book *Irrational Exuberance*, warning that the market was priced for a fall, and over the next two and a half years the index lost nearly half its value.

## Where the ten-year average goes wrong

Looking back ten years only makes sense when a business stays roughly the same over those years, which is why the Shiller P/E is meant for a broad index and not for a single stock that is volatile or growing fast. If a company has grown fivefold in a few years, its profits from eight years ago were tiny, and averaging them in drags the ten-year profit down, so the company looks far more expensive than it really is. If a company is shrinking, the old and bigger profits do the opposite and make it look cheaper than it really is.

Even the S&P 500 has changed since 2010, as fast-growing tech companies that keep a large share of their sales as profit have become a bigger part of the index. The Shiller P/E has stayed above its long-term average of 17 every month since August 2009 and stood at about 39 in November 2026, so anyone who waited for it to look cheap again missed a rise of more than six and a half times in the index since the start of 2010.

The Shiller P/E is good at seeing through one unusual year, a crash or a boom, but it can only tell you something when the companies behind it earn their money much the same way they did ten years ago.

title: Dollar-cost averaging through the 2008 crash
summary: You buy the S&P 500 at its 2007 record, right before the crash, and keep adding $500 a month. By November 2026 your $124,500 is worth about $573,000.
youtubeTitle: Buying the 2007 top on purpose
body:
What keeps a lot of people out of the stock market is the fear of buying right at the top and then watching half the money disappear. So imagine doing exactly that, on purpose, at the top before the biggest crash since the Great Depression. On 9 October 2007 the S&P 500, an index of 500 big American companies, closed at a record high.

That day you put $10,000 into a fund that buys the whole index, and from then on you add another $500 at the start of every month, whatever happens. All the values below assume that the dividends, the part of their profits the companies pay out to their owners, go back into the fund, and they leave out fees and taxes.

## Buying all the way down

Within a year the investment bank Lehman Brothers went bust, and since nobody knew which bank would be next, investors rushed to sell their shares and put the money somewhere safe. By March 2009 the index was 57 percent below its record.

By then you had put in $18,500, and it was worth $9,582, about half.

Every month the news was worse, and every new payment felt like good money thrown after bad, but the cheaper the index got, the more of it each payment bought, and the one at the start of March 2009 bought more than twice as much as the same money would have bought on the day of the record.

## The best days came during the panic

Nobody knew at the time that 9 March was the bottom, and the very next day the index jumped more than 6 percent, one of its ten best days since the record. Days like that come in the middle of a panic, just when you most want out, and six of those ten came between October 2008 and March 2009, while the crash was at its worst.

They also carry a huge part of the gains. The $10,000 you put in on the record day, left alone, had grown to about $67,000 by November 2026, but if it had missed just those ten days out of almost five thousand, it would have grown to only about $30,000.

## A year after the bottom

By April 2010, a year after the bottom, the index was still about a quarter below its record, and yet your account was already worth a bit more than everything you'd put in. The $10,000 from the record day, on its own, was still worth only about $8,100, so it was the cheap months that had pulled you back above water.

Putting in the same amount every month whatever the price is called dollar-cost averaging. A fixed amount buys more of the index when prices are low and less when they're high, so the months that feel the worst are the ones that buy the most, and you need only part of the fall to be made up before you have your money back.

## The score after nineteen years

By 17 November 2026 you had put in $124,500, and the account was worth about $573,000.

Someone who saw the crash coming would have kept the money in a savings account (one paying the interest rate on three-month US government bills), put it all in at the close on the day of the bottom and then kept adding every month, and they would have about $711,000. But they would have had to know that this one record was the top, when it looked like any other record. Since March 2013 the index has closed at a record 470 times, and none of those records was followed by a fall as deep as the one after 2007. They would also have had to buy on the day the news was at its worst.

What happens far more often is that the fear of the top keeps people out altogether. The same payments, made into that savings account instead, would be worth about $154,000.

So the person who knew the future ended up about $138,000 ahead of you, and the person who stayed out for fear of buying the top ended up about $419,000 behind you, which is about three times what buying the top cost you.

title: Implied volatility term structure and skew
summary: A stock has no single implied volatility. Meta's options show why: options that run past earnings and puts that protect against a fall are priced higher.
youtubeTitle: Why one stock has many implied volatilities
body:
If you look up Meta's implied volatility, you get one number, and at the close on 18 November 2026, with the stock at $619, that number was about 41 percent. That's usually the figure for just one kind of option, though, the ones that run for about a month and are at the money, so their strike sits right at today's price. Every other option on Meta has an implied volatility of its own, and they differ in two ways, by how long the option runs and by how far its strike is from where the stock is now. If you only go by the one number, some of them cost quite a bit more than you'd expect.

## Longer options and the earnings date

If you compare at-the-money options with different expiration dates, what traders call the term structure, here is what Meta looked like that day:

- 18 December 2026: 41 percent
- 15 January 2027: 39 percent
- 19 February 2027: 42 percent
- 21 May 2027: 43 percent
- 17 December 2027: 43 percent
- 15 December 2028: 43 percent

The options that end in December or in mid-January sit at around 40 percent, but from February on they're all at 42 or 43. What happens in between is that Meta reports its earnings for the last quarter of the year around the end of January. It did so on 1 February 2024, 29 January 2025 and 28 January 2026, and the date for the next one hasn't been announced yet.

After earnings, Meta has moved by more than 10 percent in a single day several times: up 20 percent in February 2024, down 10.5 percent in April 2024, up 11 percent in July 2025 and down 11 percent in October 2025. Implied volatility is like an average over the option's whole life, so one wild day lifts every option that's still running when it comes. And because Meta reports every three months, the longer options always have a few of those days in them, which keeps them up at 42 or 43 percent as well.

You can also run this backwards and ask how big a move the market is pricing in for earnings day. If you take January's 39 percent as the stock's ordinary level, the step up to 42 percent in February is what you get when that one extra day is expected to move the stock by about 8 percent, up or down. Put four days like that into a year on top of the 39 percent and you land at about 42 percent, which is roughly where the long-dated options sit.

## Puts, calls and the volatility skew

Now take the December options, which all end on the same day, and line them up by strike instead, and you get what's called the volatility skew. A put with a strike around $557, so that it only pays if Meta falls more than 10 percent by then, has an implied volatility of 45 percent, while a call that only pays if Meta climbs more than 10 percent has just 39. That's because stocks tend to climb slowly and fall fast, and lots of investors buy puts as insurance against exactly that kind of fall, so the people selling those puts can ask more for them. December isn't an exception either, because in every expiry on the list above, the put 10 percent below the price has a higher implied volatility than the call 10 percent above it.

## What the skew costs

The difference costs real money. If that December put were priced at the 41 percent you looked up, it would cost about $6.65 per share. At its own 45 percent it costs about $8.50, so the insurance is over a quarter more expensive, about 28 percent, than the one number would make you think, and since a contract usually covers 100 shares, that's around $850 instead of $665 for a single contract. The 41 percent on the quote page describes the one-month option at today's price, so whenever you buy anything else, a longer option or a put to protect against a fall, the price you pay is set by that option's own implied volatility, and that can sit well above the one number you looked up.

title: Great Recession vs Great Depression
summary: The Great Depression started in 1929 and left one in four Americans out of work; the Great Recession of 2007 to 2009 peaked at one in ten.
youtubeTitle: Great Recession vs Great Depression, explained
body:
People mix up the Great Depression and the Great Recession all the time because the two names sound almost identical, even though they happened nearly eighty years apart and one was far worse than the other.

The Great Depression began with the Wall Street stock market crash of October 1929 and dragged on for more than ten years. At its worst in 1933, US unemployment hit 24.9 percent, meaning roughly one in every four American workers had no job, and total economic output had fallen by more than a quarter. Unemployment stayed near or above ten percent all the way through 1941.

The Great Recession came from the US subprime housing and banking crash between December 2007 and June 2009. It was the deepest downturn since the Second World War, and it was brutal for millions of families, but it lasted a year and a half rather than a decade. Total output fell by a little over four percent, and unemployment peaked at ten percent, or one in ten workers, in October 2009.

## What a recession and a depression actually mean

In economics, a recession simply means the economy as a whole is shrinking instead of growing: people buy less, businesses produce less, and workers get laid off. The popular rule of thumb, set out in a 1974 *New York Times* article by Bureau of Labor Statistics commissioner Julius Shiskin, is that an economy is in a recession once its total output shrinks for two quarters in a row, which is six months. In the United States, the National Bureau of Economic Research looks more broadly at employment, real income, industrial production, sales, and gross domestic product across the whole economy when dating a recession.
