A depression, on the other hand, has no official cutoff number or textbook threshold at all. It is simply a recession that cuts much deeper and drags on for years. That is why an old joke from the 1950s, first recorded in print from Teamsters union president Dave Beck in 1954, popularized by former president Harry Truman in 1958, and reused by Ronald Reagan on the 1980 campaign trail, says that a recession is when your neighbour loses his job, and a depression is when you lose yours.

## How each word started as the softer one

The reason there is no neat boundary between a recession and a depression is that neither term began as a strict measurement. Each one started out as a softer word meant to avoid scaring the public.

Throughout the 1800s and early 1900s, severe financial crashes were called panics, such as the Panic of 1873 or the Panic of 1907, because depositors literally panicked and ran to pull their money out of the banks. Politicians disliked the word panic because using it only created more fear. When the stock market crashed in 1929, President Herbert Hoover and other officials leaned on a calmer-sounding word that had been used on and off since President James Monroe's time for a period of sluggish trade: a depression.

As the 1930s dragged on, the word depression stopped sounding calm and became the most frightening word in politics. When the economy finally began recovering and then tumbled again in 1937 and 1938, nobody in Washington wanted to tell voters they were sliding back into a depression. Instead, a milder word that economist Wesley Clair Mitchell had used in technical business-cycle research took over in everyday language for an ordinary downturn: a recession, just a temporary step back.

Seventy years later, that same habit gave the 2008 financial crisis its name. Calling the downturn of 2007 to 2009 the Great Recession was a way to say in two words that it was the worst economic slump since the 1930s, while still making clear that it never reached the scale of the Great Depression.

title: Bonds explained
summary: A bond is simply a loan sliced into small pieces so ordinary investors can lend money to a company or government in return for steady interest.
youtubeTitle: Bonds explained: why a bond is just a loan
body:
When a company or a government needs to borrow a lot of money, say to build a new factory or a highway, it doesn't have to walk into a bank and ask for a single giant loan. Instead, it can slice that big loan into thousands of small pieces and borrow the money straight from ordinary investors. Each of those pieces is called a **bond**, so when you buy a bond, all you're really doing is lending your money to the company or the government that issued it.

## How the payments work: coupon and maturity

Say you buy a ten-year bond from a company for $1,000 that pays 4 percent interest a year. Buying that bond means you've lent the company $1,000 upfront, and in return they promise to make two sets of payments to you over the life of the loan:

- **The coupon:** Every year for ten years, the company pays you 4 percent of your $1,000 loan, which comes out to $40 a year. In bond language, that regular annual interest payment is called the **coupon**.
- **Maturity:** When the ten years are up, at what's called **maturity**, the loan comes due and the company pays you back your full $1,000 principal.

Over the whole ten years, you collect ten yearly payments of $40, which makes $400 in interest, plus your original $1,000 back at the end.

## How a bond differs from a stock

Being a lender makes owning a bond very different from owning a **stock**. When you buy a stock, you become a part-owner of the company, which means your return is tied directly to how the business performs. If the company takes off and doubles in value, your stock goes up with it, and if the business does badly, your stock falls.

With a bond, you're not an owner at all but a **lender**. Even if the company becomes ten times bigger over the next decade, you don't share in that upside; you still only get your $40 a year and your $1,000 back at maturity.

On the other hand, the company has a legal obligation to pay you that interest whether it had a great year or a terrible one. And if the company ever goes bust, **bondholders are first in line** for whatever money is left over from selling off the business, before shareholders get a single cent.

## Why some bonds pay more than others

Being first in line doesn't make a bond risk-free, because if a bankrupt company doesn't have enough left over to cover its debts, bondholders can still lose their money. So just like with any other loan, the interest rate a bond pays depends on how safe the borrower is.

When you lend to the US government by buying a **Treasury bond**, you're almost guaranteed to get your money back, so the government only has to pay a few percent a year to find willing lenders, around 4 percent on a ten-year Treasury. When you lend to a shaky company that might go bankrupt before the ten years are up, it has to offer a much higher interest rate, sometimes 8 or 10 percent a year on what people call a **junk bond**, just to convince anyone to take the risk. Whether a bond pays a little or a lot, though, the deal behind it is always the same: you're the lender, you collect steady interest along the way, and as long as the borrower holds up, you get your loan back at the end.

title: What made Steve Eisman famous
summary: In 2006 Steve Eisman followed the other side of his subprime mortgage bet, uncovered Wall Street's nested CDO machine, and more than doubled his fund.
youtubeTitle: What made Steve Eisman famous
body:
In 2006, at the height of the American housing boom, an outspoken New York hedge fund manager named Steve Eisman didn't just bet that bad mortgages would fail. He bet that Wall Street would blow itself up with them.

Before starting the FrontPoint Financial Services Fund, Eisman had spent years as an analyst covering subprime mortgage lenders. He already knew they were handing out home loans to borrowers without checking their income, and then selling those loans by the thousands to big Wall Street banks. What he wanted to understand was how those risky loans were being packaged, and who on earth was buying them.

## How a mortgage bond gets sliced into layers

The banks that bought those subprime mortgages didn't just hold them as plain loans. They bundled thousands of them together into a single mortgage bond and sliced that bond into layers, called tranches, from top to bottom.

When homeowners paid their mortgages each month, the cash flowed into the top layer first, while any losses from people who defaulted hit the bottom layers first. Because the top layer was the last to take a hit, rating agencies gave it a triple-A safety rating, the same grade given to United States government debt. Meanwhile, a risky bottom slice, rated triple-B, sat right near the firing line and would be wiped out completely if only about eight percent of the homeowners stopped paying.

## Betting against the bottom slices

When a trader at Deutsche Bank, Greg Lippmann, showed Eisman that he could bet directly against those triple-B mortgage slices using a kind of insurance contract called a credit default swap, Eisman piled in.

Insuring $100 million of triple-B mortgage bonds cost a yearly fee of about $2 million, or roughly two percent a year. As long as the bonds kept paying, that fee was gone, but if the homeowners defaulted and the triple-B slices went bust, the contract paid out the full $100 million. By early 2007 Eisman had put $300 million of those bets on, and one question kept nagging at him: who was eager enough to keep taking the other side?

## A contract inside a CDO inside a mortgage bond

The banks had found a trick for those triple-B slices that hardly anyone wanted to buy on their own. They gathered leftover triple-B slices from dozens of different mortgage bonds, packed them into a brand-new box called a CDO, or collateralized debt obligation, and paid rating agencies like Moody's and S&P to rate the new package. Because the rating agencies didn't want to lose the banks' business, they stamped roughly 80 percent of that bundle of risky slices as triple-A, hiding subprime loans inside a package that big banks and pension funds eagerly bought as ultra-safe debt.

At a mortgage industry conference in Las Vegas in January 2007, a CDO manager named Wing Chau happily explained the next layer to Eisman over dinner. Whenever Eisman bought insurance betting that a mortgage bond would fail, managers like Chau took the other side of that contract and packed the insurance contracts themselves into yet another box, called a synthetic CDO. The buyers of a synthetic CDO collected Eisman's yearly insurance fees, but had to pay out the full amount if the underlying loans went bust.

By that point, the product was a contract inside a CDO inside a mortgage bond. It was nested so deep that $50 million of real home loans could carry billions of dollars in side bets stacked on top, and almost nobody on Wall Street besides Eisman could see through the mess anymore.

## When every nested layer collapsed

Eisman walked out of Las Vegas realizing that the rating agencies stamping those packages triple-A, and the big banks holding billions of dollars of them on their own books without seeing the risk inside, would collapse right along with the loans. He raised his insurance bets against subprime bonds from $300 million to $550 million, and shorted the shares of Moody's, S&P, UBS and Lehman Brothers, betting that their stock prices would plunge once the losses surfaced.

When homeowners started defaulting in large numbers later that year, the bottom slices vanished and every nested layer above them collapsed too. Investors dumped bank shares, Lehman Brothers eventually went bankrupt, and by the end of 2007 Eisman's fund at FrontPoint had more than doubled from about $700 million to $1.5 billion. The sharpest contrast sat under his own roof: FrontPoint had been bought in late 2006 by Morgan Stanley, and while Eisman was more than doubling his fund inside the bank by betting against triple-A CDOs, another trading desk at Morgan Stanley lost $9 billion holding the very packages everyone had sworn could never fail.

title: Three kinds of leverage, explained with $1,000
summary: You don't need a bank loan to multiply your returns. Margin, call options, and leveraged ETFs each deliver leverage, but each comes with a completely different trap.
youtubeTitle: Three kinds of leverage, explained with $1,000
body:
When most people hear the word leverage, they picture borrowing money from a broker. But in finance, leverage simply means any structure where your profit or loss moves by a multiple of the underlying asset. 

Borrowing is only one way to achieve that. There are three completely different mechanisms to turn a small move into a large gain, and each one fails in a completely different way. To see how they compare, imagine you have $1,000 to invest in a stock currently trading at $100.

## 1. Margin: borrowing money with collateral

The traditional method is buying on margin. Your broker lends you money to buy extra shares and holds your own cash as collateral. That cash is your margin, the cushion that protects the broker if the stock falls.

Suppose you put up your $1,000, borrow $4,000 from the broker, and buy 50 shares at $100 for a total of $5,000. Because you control $5,000 with $1,000 of your own, you are five times leveraged.

If the stock rises 10 percent to $110, those 50 shares are worth $5,500. You repay the $4,000 loan, and you are left with $1,500. That is a 50 percent gain on your money from a 10 percent move in the stock.

The trap is what happens on the downside. If the stock drops 20 percent to $80, the shares are worth exactly $4,000. The broker takes every dollar of it to pay off the loan, and your $1,000 is completely wiped out. If the stock falls further, you can even end up owing money you never had. But you usually don't get the chance to hold on: as soon as your collateral cushion thins out, the broker issues a margin call, and if you don't add more cash, they liquidate your shares right at the bottom.

## 2. Call options: contractual leverage without a loan

Options give you leverage through a legal contract rather than borrowed money. A call option gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy a share at a fixed strike price before an expiration date.

With that same $1,000, instead of borrowing, you could buy 200 call options at $5 each, giving you the right to buy shares at a strike of $100. If the stock rises 10 percent to $110, each option gives you the right to buy a $110 share for $100. At expiration, each contract is worth $10. Your 200 contracts are now worth $2,000, doubling your money for a 100 percent gain.

The huge advantage over margin is that you never took a loan. Even if the company goes bankrupt and the stock collapses to zero, you can never lose more than the $1,000 premium you paid. There is no broker debt, no margin call, and no forced liquidation.

The trap here is time decay. Options have an expiration date. If the stock stays flat at $100 until expiry, your options expire completely worthless, and your $1,000 is gone. With a margin loan, a flat stock only costs you interest while you wait; with an option, time running out is lethal.

## 3. Leveraged ETFs: daily resets and volatility drag

The third way is buying a leveraged exchange-traded fund, like a 3x S&P 500 fund. There is no margin account, no loan, and no expiration date. You buy and sell it on the exchange just like an ordinary share.

The trap is how the fund creates that leverage: it resets its exposure at the end of every single trading day. Over two days, that daily compounding can quietly destroy your capital even if the index ends up right where it started.

Imagine you put $100 into an ordinary index, and $100 into a 3x leveraged version. On day one, the index rises 10 percent to $110. The 3x fund jumps 30 percent, to $130. 

On day two, the index drops 10 percent. Ten percent of $110 is $11, so the index finishes at $99, down just 1 percent over the two days. But the 3x fund loses 30 percent of its new, higher value: 30 percent of $130 is $39, leaving you with $91. The index barely moved, but you lost 9 percent. 

This effect is known as volatility drag or beta slippage. In a choppy, sideways market, daily rebalancing constantly buys high and sells low, grinding your capital down over time.

## Which trap fits your bet?

All three tools multiply returns, but each shifts the risk into a different dimension:
- **Margin** risks sudden liquidation and debt when prices fall.
- **Options** cap your dollar loss, but put you on a ticking clock.
- **Leveraged ETFs** remove both the loan and the clock, but bleed money when the market goes sideways.

Understanding leverage isn't just knowing how big the wins can be; it's knowing which trap you've agreed to step into.

title: Elon Musk is a trillionaire, what does that mean?
summary: SpaceX's June 2026 IPO briefly took Elon Musk past $1.4 trillion. Comparing that fortune to American households shows what wealth at that scale buys.
youtubeTitle: Elon Musk is a trillionaire, what does that mean?
body:
On June 12, 2026, SpaceX went public on the Nasdaq, and for a moment Elon Musk's net worth shot past $1.4 trillion, making him the first trillionaire in human history. Because most of that fortune sits in shares of SpaceX and Tesla, stock swings soon cooled it back toward $850 billion. Even so, crossing a trillion dollars raises a plain question about what happens to a country when one person holds that much wealth.

## One fortune next to a third of America

One way to picture a trillion dollars is to look at the Federal Reserve's household wealth data. At a trillion dollars, Musk alone holds roughly as much net worth as 120 million Americans combined, more than a third of the United States. If you lined up every person in the country, over a third of that crowd would have to pool everything they own, after subtracting their debts, just to match one man.

There is a catch with that comparison, and it is worth being honest about it. Net worth is everything a household owns minus everything it owes. According to the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, the poorest quarter of American households, around 33.5 million families, add up to less than zero. Their average net worth is minus $4,300, because student loans, car loans, and credit card balances wipe out whatever savings or assets they have.

When you add households up from the bottom of the distribution, millions of families in debt cancel out millions of families above them who have modest savings. That makes it surprisingly easy to reach a huge headcount. Technically, if you have a single dollar in your pocket and no debt, you hold more net worth than the entire bottom quarter of American households combined.

## Throwing out the debt math

Dropping everyone in debt does not make a trillion dollars look any smaller. Compare it instead to families sitting right in the middle of America. The Federal Reserve puts the median American household's net worth at $215,900, or about $216,000. Divide a trillion dollars by $215,900, and one trillionaire still equals more than 4.5 million middle-class families put together.

At that level, money stops working the way it does for ordinary people. Nobody can spend a trillion dollars on houses, cars, or yachts. Once a fortune gets that big, it stops buying everyday things and starts buying assets and influence.

## What billionaire money buys

Even before SpaceX took him past a trillion, Musk showed what that kind of money buys in practice. In 2022 he led a $44 billion buyout of Twitter, taking control of one of the world's largest public squares. In 2024 he poured roughly $300 million into the federal election, making him the single largest individual political donor in the United States.

By early 2025 he had a seat inside the federal government itself, running an office tasked with cutting public agencies. One of the targets was the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal watchdog that handled consumer complaints about car loans and payment apps, whose enforcement work was halted and whose Washington headquarters was closed. All of that happened while Musk's own companies, SpaceX and Tesla, had relied on more than $38 billion in federal contracts, loans, subsidies, and tax credits over two decades.

## The price of power at a trillion dollars

Next to a trillion dollars, repeating that playbook barely leaves a dent. Paying $44 billion for a global platform is less than 5 percent of a trillion. Spending $300 million to become America's biggest political donor is 0.03 percent of a trillion, which for a middle-class family worth $216,000 is the same share of wealth as spending about $65 on dinner.

Musk is the first person to cross the trillion-dollar mark, but he is only the front runner of a whole class. On the 2026 Forbes 400 list, the 400 richest Americans held $8 trillion between them, with the top 20 alone holding $4 trillion. When a small group of billionaires grows that rich, buying the town square, bankrolling national elections, and dismantling the agencies meant to watch their companies costs them what feels like pocket change, and everyone else is left living with the rules they help write.

title: Passive vs active investing
summary: Active investors try to beat the stock market while passive index funds match it, and simple math plus lower fees usually put passive ahead.
youtubeTitle: Passive vs active investing: why index funds usually win
body:
When you put $10,000 into the stock market, you face a basic choice: do you try to beat the market, or do you just own all of it?

Trying to beat the market is called **active investing**. You can do it yourself by researching and picking individual stocks, or you can pay a fund manager to study companies and trade on your behalf. The other approach is **passive investing**. Instead of picking winners, you buy an **index fund**, which automatically owns a small slice of every company on a set market list called an **index**, such as the S&P 500 for the 500 largest American companies.

Active investing tries to outsmart the market while passive investing settles for matching it, so at first glance you might expect paid professionals with research teams to come out ahead.

## Why active investors as a group cannot beat the market

The catch starts with simple arithmetic, a point the economist William F. Sharpe spelled out in 1991. Every share in the stock market is owned by someone. Because passive index funds hold a matching slice of every company in the market, they earn the market's average return by definition.

Once you set aside what passive funds own, all the active investors together hold the remaining shares, which have the exact same mix of companies as the whole market. Before costs, active investors as a group earn the exact same average return as the market itself. For every active dollar that beats the average, another active dollar has to fall behind it.

## How a small yearly fee turns into $22,000

Fees are what tip the scale. Active funds pay analysts, researchers, and traders, so they take a yearly fee straight out of your money whether the fund goes up or down, often around 1 percent a year for retail stock funds. A passive index fund just copies a list automatically, so it can charge around 0.1 percent a year instead.

One percent sounds small until you follow $10,000 over 30 years in a typical stock market returning 8 percent a year on average before fees. In the passive fund charging 0.1 percent a year, you keep a 7.9 percent return and your $10,000 grows to $97,869, almost **$98,000**. In an active fund charging 1 percent a year, even if the manager matches the market every single year before costs, that fee pulls your return down to 7 percent and leaves you with $76,123, about **$76,000**.

That is a gap of $21,746, nearly **$22,000**. Around $8,300 of that gap comes from the higher direct fees, and the remaining $13,400 is the future compounding growth those fees would have earned if they had stayed invested. Just to tie the passive fund, an active manager has to beat the market by 0.9 percentage points every year.

## What happens in real life

Over long stretches, very few managers pull that off. S&P Dow Jones Indices tracks how professional American stock funds perform against the S&P 500 in its SPIVA scorecards. Over the 20 years through 2024, 92 percent of active US large-company funds (more than nine out of ten) ended up doing worse than simply owning the S&P 500. Those managers are competing against other smart professionals watching the exact same companies, all while carrying a much heavier fee every year.

## Where passive investing stops working

Passive investing still has clear limits. Because an index fund copies the market automatically, you give up any chance of beating it, and the fund cannot avoid an overpriced stock or step aside into cash during a crash. It holds every company on the list all the way up and all the way down.

Passive investing also depends on active buyers and sellers to work at all. Index funds buy shares at whatever price the market sets without checking what a business is worth, so active investors studying companies and arguing over prices are the ones who keep stock prices grounded in reality. Active investing keeps the market honest, yet for most ordinary investors, passive investing comes out ahead because the math and the fees put the odds heavily on its side.

title: Gary Stevenson, the trader who bet on broke families
summary: Gary Stevenson made millions at Citibank betting broke families would trap UK interest rates near zero, then quit to warn about compounding wealth.
youtubeTitle: Gary Stevenson, the trader who bet on broke families
body:
After the 2008 financial crash, the Bank of England cut interest rates from 5 percent down to 0.5 percent. On Citibank's trading floor in London, almost every banker expected the economy to bounce back quickly and interest rates to climb back toward normal. One young trader disagreed. Gary Stevenson had grown up in a working-class neighborhood in East London, and when he went home he saw ordinary families with nothing left to spend.

If regular people stop spending, businesses stall and the economy cannot get moving on its own. A central bank in that position cannot raise interest rates without making loans more expensive and crashing the economy again. So while his wealthy colleagues bet on higher rates, Stevenson took the other side and bet that interest rates would stay stuck near zero.

## The trade that paid off for a decade

Stevenson was right. The Bank of England kept its rate at 0.5 percent until August 2016, and UK rates stayed below 1 percent for thirteen years, until May 2022. His trades made tens of millions of dollars for Citibank, including roughly $35 million in 2011 by his own account in his 2024 memoir, *The Trading Game*. In his biggest year, he says his personal bonus reached about $2.5 million.

That left him a multimillionaire in his mid-twenties, and miserable. Every time his trade paid off, it meant families like the ones he grew up with were falling further behind. Eventually he walked away from banking to explain to ordinary people what he had been watching from the inside, turning his warning into a bestselling book and a YouTube channel with more than 1.5 million subscribers.

## Where the money actually goes

His main argument is easy to follow, which is a big reason so many people listen to him. When an ordinary worker gets paid, almost every pound or dollar goes straight to rent, groceries, and bills, flowing back up to landlords and large companies. When someone who is already very rich gets another million, they do not buy ten times as many groceries. They buy assets: houses, stocks, and government debt.

Run that loop for a few decades and all that money chasing the same supply of assets pushes prices out of reach for anyone living on a wage. You can see the shift in England's housing data. According to the Office for National Statistics, a typical home cost about 3.5 times a median full-time annual salary in 1997. By 2025, with median home prices around £300,000 against median full-time earnings of £39,300, the ratio stood at 7.6 times. Working a normal full-time job simply stopped keeping up with already owning property and stocks.

## The wealth tax debate

Stevenson's proposed fix is an annual wealth tax on the super-rich, taxing what they own each year instead of leaning so heavily on taxing wages. Economists push back on parts of his platform, and some of that pushback rests on real history. In 1990, twelve European OECD countries levied an annual net wealth tax. Nine of them later dropped or narrowed it, including Sweden, Germany, Austria, and France (which replaced its broad wealth tax with one limited to real estate in 2018), leaving only Switzerland, Norway, and Spain with broad European wealth taxes.

Stevenson does not ignore that track record. It is why he keeps stressing proper implementation, arguing that a wealth tax only works when governments close loopholes and focus on physical assets like land and property that nobody can pack up and move to a tax haven.

You can argue over whether a wealth tax is the right tool, or whether governments would ever pass one cleanly enough to make it stick. What is much harder to dispute is the compounding math behind his warning. Once wealth grows in assets faster than wages can grow, the richest owners naturally end up holding a larger share of everything while people living on paychecks fall further behind, and nothing in the system reverses that on its own.

title: "Tulip mania: when one bulb cost as much as a house"
summary: In 1637 a single tulip bulb sold for the price of a house in Amsterdam, yet surviving Dutch records show zero tulip bankruptcies.
youtubeTitle: Tulip mania: when one bulb cost as much as a house
body:
In early February 1637, an auction in the Dutch town of Alkmaar sold off the tulip collection of a late innkeeper named Wouter Winkel for his orphaned children. One prized lot, a bulb of the Admirael van Enkhuizen variety with an offset, fetched 5,200 guilders. At the time, a skilled craftsman earned about 300 guilders a year, and 5,000 guilders was enough to buy a comfortable canal house in Amsterdam.

That same week, the landscape painter Jan van Goyen was also buying tulips. In late January and early February he signed private deals with Allert Claesz van Ravesteyn, a former mayor of The Hague, agreeing to pay later in guilders along with one of his own paintings. Those deals left him owing nearly 900 guilders, almost three years of a craftsman's pay. Neither town knew yet that a short distance away in Haarlem, the market had already stopped dead. Yet when prices collapsed across the Netherlands, surviving archives do not show a single bankruptcy caused by tulips.

## Why the bulbs were rare

The tulips people fought over were not ordinary garden flowers. Tulips were still new to Europe, and wealthy Dutch merchants collected the rarest varieties the way collectors buy fine art. The most coveted flowers grew sharp, flame-like stripes across their petals.

Nobody in the 1630s knew what caused those patterns. Scientists only identified the cause in 1928: a plant virus, now called the tulip breaking virus. The virus distorted the flower's pigment and weakened the plant at the same time. An infected bulb could not pass its striped pattern on through seeds, and it multiplied slowly underground through small side bulbs called offsets. Supply stayed tight even when rich buyers wanted more.

## The wind trade

Rarity alone could make a flower expensive, but it takes something else to push a bulb to the price of a house. Tulip bulbs stay buried all winter and can only be dug up during the summer harvest. Rather than waiting for summer, speculators gathered in taverns through the winter of 1636 and 1637 to trade futures contracts: paper promises to buy a bulb in summer at a price locked in on the spot.

Almost no cash changed hands up front. Without real money on the table, it is easy to bid far more than you own, because you have no plan to pay in summer. You only need someone else to buy your paper promise for more before delivery arrives. Locals called this the wind trade, or windhandel, because traders were trading air.

## The auction where nobody bid

A chain of promises works only as long as the next buyer keeps showing up. Around 3 February 1637, at a tavern auction in Haarlem, sellers offered bulbs and the room went quiet. Nobody bid. Once traders realized they might actually be forced to pay house-sized sums in summer for flowers nobody else wanted, buyers vanished. News moved slowly between towns back then, so Van Goyen signed his 4 February contract and the Alkmaar orphanage auction went through on 5 February right before prices fell apart everywhere.

When it came time to settle, tavern buyers simply refused to pay. Before summer delivery arrived, on 27 April 1637, the States of Holland suspended the contracts so towns could sort out the mess. A year later, in May 1638, Haarlem's city council ruled that buyers could cancel informal tavern deals by paying 3.5 percent of the contract price. On a 5,000-guilder tavern promise, a buyer could walk away for 175 guilders. Other Dutch towns pushed similar cut-rate settlements. Tavern sellers lost paper profits they had never collected, while growers who had already sold real bulbs for cash in earlier seasons kept their money.

## What the archives actually show

The historian Anne Goldgar spent years checking seventeenth-century Dutch notary records, court files, and bankruptcy lists. She found only 37 people on record who ever spent more than a craftsman's yearly wage of 300 guilders on tulips, and she did not find a single person bankrupted by them. The famous stories of ordinary families losing everything came largely from moralizing, satirical pamphlets printed in 1637, which later writers such as Charles Mackay in 1841 treated as straight journalism.

The city settlements did not erase formal private deals signed outside the tavern trade. When Ravesteyn died in 1641, his estate records showed that Jan van Goyen still owed him 897 guilders for tulips along with a painting of Judas valued at 36 guilders. Even Van Goyen kept painting for nearly twenty more years until his death in 1656, and the 18,000 guilders of debt he left behind came mostly from bad real estate bets, not flowers. Most of the wild winter bids had only ever existed on paper, so when buyers walked away, the wider Dutch economy barely noticed.

title: What are stock index points?
summary: Stock index points are units on an arbitrary scoreboard, not dollars. Here is what 5,000 points means and why percentage moves matter more.
youtubeTitle: What are stock index points? Why a 500-point drop can be a crash or a normal day
body:
When the financial news says a stock index sits at 5,000 points, it is fair to wonder what a point is measuring. It is not a dollar, and it is not a share.

A single stock has one share price in dollars, so quoting it is straightforward. A stock **index** tracks a whole basket of companies at once, such as the S&P 500 tracking 500 large American companies whose individual share prices are all over the place. You cannot give that entire basket one dollar price. Instead, the people who build an index start a scoreboard on day one at a neat number, say 100, and call the units **points** because they are not dollars.

## How an index reaches 5,000 points

From day one onward, the scoreboard moves up and down by the same percentage as the stocks inside it. If those companies double in value, the index doubles from 100 to 200 points. If over the decades the basket grows to fifty times its starting value, the index reaches 5,000 points.

Having a running number like that lets you track a market across years and decades without juggling daily percentage changes in your head. On its own, though, 5,000 points is not a price tag for anything. It only tells you how far that specific scoreboard has climbed since it began.

## Why almost nobody cares about the raw number

Because every index chooses its own starting level and calculation method, an absolute point number says nothing about whether stocks are cheap, expensive, or even how large the market is.

That is also why comparing two different indexes by their raw points makes no sense. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sits in the tens of thousands of points, while the S&P 500 sits in the thousands. On 17 May 2024, the day the Dow first closed above 40,000 at 40,003.59, the S&P 500 closed at 5,303.27. That did not mean the Dow was more than seven times bigger or stronger. In fact, the S&P 500 tracks 500 companies while the Dow only tracks 30. The Dow started back in 1896 at 40.94 points based on share prices, whereas the S&P 500 set its 1941 to 1943 base period to 10 points based on company market values. A point level only means something when you compare the same index against its own past.

## Why headlines still shout about points

If the percentage change is the only number that tells you how big a move was, why does the news still run headlines saying the Dow plunged 500 points instead of saying it fell 1 percent? Mostly habit and drama. A 500-point drop sounds alarming and grabs attention, whereas a 1 percent move sounds routine.

The catch is that as an index climbs over the decades, each single point becomes a much smaller slice of the total. On Black Monday, 19 October 1987, the Dow started near 2,250 points (having closed the previous Friday at 2,246.74) and dropped 508 points in a single session to finish at 1,738.74. That wiped out 22.6 percent of the index in one day, still the worst single-day percentage crash in its history. Once the Dow is sitting around 40,000 points, that same 500-point drop is only 1.25 percent, which is a completely normal bumpy day in the stock market.

Points are handy for keeping a running score over time and marking round milestones, yet on their own they cannot tell you how much money anyone made or lost. Whenever you want to know what actually happened to the market, skip the raw points and look at the percentage instead.

title: TER (total expense ratio)
summary: The total expense ratio (TER) is a fund's yearly fee, taken out daily so you never see a bill. Over 30 years, 0.07% vs 1.5% costs a third of your money.
youtubeTitle: TER (total expense ratio) explained: the fund fee you never see
body:
When you put money into a fund, the company running it charges a yearly fee called the **TER**, short for total expense ratio. That percentage pays for the fund's ongoing running costs, such as management, administration, custody, auditing, legal work, and any index licensing fees.

The tricky part is how you pay it. You never get an invoice, and nothing ever leaves your bank account. Instead, the fund takes a tiny slice straight out of the money inside the fund every single day, whether the market goes up or down. Your share is just worth a little less than it would have been, so you barely notice.

## Seven dollars versus a hundred and fifty

Say you invest $10,000 in the stock market and look at two different stock funds. A simple **index fund** that tracks the market automatically might charge a TER of 0.07 percent a year, which is what large S&P 500 ETFs such as Vanguard VUAA and iShares CSPX charge. On $10,000, that comes to $7 in the first year. An **actively managed fund**, where human managers pick the stocks, might charge 1.5 percent a year, a common ongoing rate for European retail active equity funds. On $10,000, that comes to $150 in year one. On paper, 1.5 percent looks small enough to brush off.

## Why 1.5 percent is much bigger than it looks

That percentage stops looking small once you compare it to what stocks actually earn. Suppose the market makes 7 percent in a year before fees. With the 0.07 percent index fund, you keep 6.93 percent, almost all of the gain, because the fee only takes 1 percent of your yearly return. With the 1.5 percent active fund, the fee comes straight off the top and leaves you with 5.5 percent. In an ordinary 7 percent year, that fee takes more than a fifth of your entire gain (21.4 percent).

In a weak year, the difference is even starker. If the stock market only rises 1 percent over the year, a 1.5 percent fee leaves you down 0.5 percent, so the fee itself is the difference between making money and losing money.

## What happens over 30 years

Now stretch that 7 percent yearly return out over 30 years, assuming both funds match the market before fees so the cheap fund nets 6.93 percent a year and the expensive one nets 5.5 percent. Your $10,000 in the 0.07 percent index fund grows to $74,643, almost $75,000. In the 1.5 percent fund, the exact same market return leaves you with $49,840, just under $50,000. The gap is $24,803, about a third of what you would have had.

Two things push that gap so far past 30 years of $150 ($4,500). First, the TER is a percentage of your whole balance, not a flat dollar fee, so as your investment grows the yearly charge grows right along with it, rising from $150 in year one to $709 in year 30 and adding up to about $10,212 more in direct fees than the cheap fund. Second, every dollar taken out of the fund can no longer stay invested and compound for you, which costs another $14,591 in lost growth on top.

## What the TER leaves out

Despite the word total, the TER does not cover every cost of owning a fund. It leaves out whatever your broker charges when you buy or sell shares, and it leaves out the trading costs the fund pays whenever it buys and sells stocks inside the portfolio.

Even so, nobody knows what the stock market will do next year or over the next thirty years, while the TER is a cost you know for sure before you put a dollar in. Whenever two funds invest in the same market, picking the one with the lower TER is the easiest way to keep more of your money.

title: Ranking 7 famous market crashes from F to S tier
summary: Seven famous market crashes from 1637 to 2020 ranked from F-tier overrated to S-tier catastrophe by what they did to ordinary people.
youtubeTitle: Ranking 7 famous market crashes from F to S tier
body:
Some famous market crashes ruined whole generations, while a couple of the most talked-about ones were mostly noise. Ranking seven of them from 1637 to 2020, from F-tier overrated to S-tier catastrophe, shows pretty quickly that the steepest drop in stock prices is not always the crash that hurts the most.

## 1637 and 1720: flowers and Isaac Newton

Start with Tulip Mania in 1637, which I put straight in F-tier. Rare bulbs really did trade on paper for 3,000 to 6,000 guilders, more than ten times a Dutch artisan's yearly pay of around 300 guilders, before prices collapsed in February 1637. The legend makes it sound like flowers sank the Netherlands. When historian Anne Goldgar checked the Amsterdam archives, though, she found almost nobody went broke, Dutch courts refused to enforce those contracts, and the Dutch economy barely noticed.

Britain's South Sea Bubble in 1720 earns C-tier from me. Shares in a hyped trading company jumped from around £128 to roughly £1,000 in six months, almost eightfold, before falling below £200 by December, a drop of over 80 percent. Even Isaac Newton got caught. Bank of England ledgers show he sold early in April for a profit, watched shares keep climbing, jumped back in near the June peak, and lost roughly £11,000 to £13,000 net, a serious fortune then. Any crash that humbles Isaac Newton deserves a spot on the list.

## 1929: the benchmark for ruin

Then 1929 hits, and I put it straight into S-tier. From September 1929 to July 1932, the Dow Jones fell 89 percent, and the index stayed below its 1929 peak for 25 years, until November 1954. What made it unbearable was what happened outside Wall Street. There was no federal guarantee on bank accounts back then, so as panic spread between 1930 and 1933, more than 9,000 American banks shut their doors. Families who had never owned a single stock watched their savings disappear, unemployment hit 24.9 percent in 1933, roughly one worker in four, and the fallout dragged the world into the Great Depression.

## 1987 and 2000: panic without broken banks

For one day in October 1987, Black Monday looked like 1929 all over again. Automated trading programs set to sell whenever prices dipped triggered a panic loop that wiped 22.6 percent off the Dow in a single session, still the worst one-day percentage drop in American market history. The next morning, Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan promised banks cash to keep lending. US stocks climbed back past their old peak in under two years, no American recession followed, and I drop Black Monday all the way to D-tier.

By 2000 the frenzy had moved to the internet, where Pets.com spent about $1.2 million on a Super Bowl ad while losing money on the dog food it sold. When reality caught up, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 78 percent between March 2000 and October 2002, and it took 15 years, until April 2015, to get back above that high. That kind of wait hurts, so I put dot-com in B-tier. Still, the banks stayed standing and the 2001 American recession lasted just eight months and stayed mild.

## 2008 and 2020: credit freezes and cheap cash

Next is 2008. The S&P 500 fell 57 percent from October 2007 to March 2009 and recovered in five and a half years, a smaller drop and a much faster comeback than dot-com. Yet I put 2008 higher, in A-tier, because reckless mortgage bets blew up major banks and froze global lending. When banks stop lending, ordinary businesses cannot borrow to make payroll or stay open. Nearly nine million Americans lost their jobs, and millions of families lost their homes to foreclosure.

Finally, 2020. Pandemic lockdowns knocked more than 20 million Americans out of work in April alone, while the S&P 500 fell 34 percent in 33 calendar days. Then the Federal Reserve slashed interest rates near zero and pumped trillions into financial markets, sending US stocks back to record highs in August, under six months from the February top. As a pure stock drop it barely lasted, yet that flood of cheap cash sent stock and housing prices soaring and shifted huge wealth toward people who already owned assets, lifting the top 1 percent's share of US household wealth from 29.9 percent in early 2020 to 32.1 percent a year later. That lasting shift puts 2020 in C-tier.

Only 1929 and 2008 end up at the top of the ranking. A wild fall in share prices can be terrifying to watch, and central banks can sometimes patch over the market panic in months, but a crash only turns into a real catastrophe once it breaks the banks and reaches ordinary people's jobs, homes, and savings.

title: What "priced in" means in the stock market
summary: Why your everyday stock hunch is usually already in the share price, how bubbles still happen anyway, and what to check before placing an order.
youtubeTitle: Priced in, explained: why your stock hunch is probably already in the price
body:
The Pope secretly launching a memecoin? Priced in. The CIA admitting every pigeon in New York is a spy drone? Priced in. A billionaire secretly cloning dinosaurs on a tax-free island? Believe it or not, the stock market has already priced it in.

Behind the joke is a simple rule about how stock prices work. Saying something is **priced in** means a share's price today already reflects everything the market knows and expects about the company's future. That sounds harmless enough until you notice how often it trips up ordinary investors. You walk into a coffee shop, love the drink, and think you should buy the stock. You try a plant-based burger that tastes good, or you start seeing layoffs around you and figure a crash is coming. It feels like a smart observation, yet almost every insight you have about the world is one the stock market has already spotted and paid for.

## Who sits on the other side of your trade

When you buy or bet against a stock on a hunch, you are not trading against other people skimming the news over breakfast. On Wall Street, dedicated analysts spend their entire week studying just ten or fifteen companies. They track supplier orders, buy anonymized credit card sales data to read revenue before a company reports it, and even look at satellite photos of retail parking lots to count cars.

Because big funds act on that data right away, the price moves long before a trend feels obvious to everyone else. Before you ever taste that coffee or burger, funds have already seen sales climbing, bought the shares, and pushed the price up to match. If layoffs are spreading, they have already sold and pushed the price down. By the time you place an order based on the same clue, you are already paying for what you just noticed.

## How a bubble can still grow in plain sight

The same thing holds for bigger stories, like everyone warning online that AI is a bubble. If you are hearing that argument everywhere, Wall Street analysts have heard it too, so that worry is already built into today's prices.

That does not mean AI cannot be a real bubble. Being priced in does not mean the market can see the future. A stock's price is only today's tug of war between believers and skeptics. Even when half the market suspects prices are too high, nobody knows whether the boom will pay off or when it might pop. Plenty of investors stay in anyway, because bubbles can climb for years and sitting on the sidelines while everyone else makes money hurts too. So a bubble can grow right out in the open, and it only crashes once the promised profits fail to show up and believers finally start selling.

## Why finding an edge is so hard

Finding new information that nobody else has noticed is hard even for professionals who are all racing against each other. Over the twenty years through December 2024, 91.99 percent of actively managed U.S. large-cap stock funds did worse than the S&P 500, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices. In the long run, more than nine out of ten professional funds that try to pick winning American stocks lose to a simple index fund that buys the five hundred biggest companies automatically.

Every once in a while, a sharp trader really does spot something the crowd missed and makes a legendary bet, only to get the next bets wrong afterward. Beating the whole market once is hard enough, and doing it consistently is even harder. So before you place your next order, pause for a second and ask yourself whether you really know something the rest of the market does not, or if it is already priced in.

title: Dividends explained
summary: A dividend is profit a company pays out in cash. The share price drops by about the same amount, so it isn't free money, yet reinvesting them adds up fast.
youtubeTitle: Dividends explained: why a dividend isn't free money
body:
When a profitable company has cash left over after paying its bills, it has to decide what to do with that money. It can put the cash back into growing the business, or it can hand some of it straight to the people who own its shares, usually a few times a year. That cash payout is called a **dividend**.

Say you own one share of a company trading at $50, and it pays a $2 dividend. Two dollars of real profit leaves the company's bank account and lands straight in yours.

## Why a dividend is not free money

Receiving $2 on a $50 stock can feel like a 4 percent bonus dropped on top of your investment, until you watch what happens to the share price. On the cutoff day when the company locks in who gets the payout (called the **ex-dividend date**), the stock usually drops by about $2, from $50 down to $48.

That drop happens because the cash is not coming out of thin air. Before the cutoff, buying a $50 share meant buying a slice of the business plus $2 of cash sitting inside it. Once that $2 is set aside to leave the company's bank account, the business itself is worth $2 a share less, so new buyers won't pay $50 anymore. You end up holding a $48 share plus $2 in cash, which is still $50 in total. A dividend doesn't create money out of nothing; it just moves cash from the company's pocket into yours.

## How reinvested dividends add up over 30 years

Because a stock drops whenever it pays a dividend, the headline price index you see in the news leaves out all the cash companies paid out along the way. If you spend those dividends as they arrive, you're pulling money out of your investment every year. If you reinvest them to buy more shares instead, those new shares grow in value and pay dividends of their own.

Take the S&P 500, the main index of big American companies, over the 30 full years from the end of 1995 to the end of 2025. On share prices alone (the price index rising from 615.93 to 6,845.50), $10,000 grew to $111,141, about 8.4 percent a year. With every dividend automatically reinvested (the total return index climbing from 792.04 to 15,220.45), that same $10,000 grew to $192,168, about 10.4 percent a year.

That is $81,027 more in the end, meaning more than 44 percent of the total gain came from reinvesting dividends. Even if you had simply kept the cash dividends sitting unspent on the side, they would only have added about $18,327 in raw cash; the rest of the gap came from buying extra shares along the way and letting them compound.

## Dividends versus share buybacks

If dividends add up to that much over decades, why don't all companies pay them? Fast-growing companies usually pay nothing, because they expect to earn more by putting that cash into new products or factories. Older, steadier businesses often bring in more cash than they can usefully reinvest, so they return the extra money to shareholders.

Some do that with dividends, while others use **share buybacks** instead, spending the cash to buy back their own shares on the market and cancel them. Imagine a $500 company made up of a $480 business plus $20 in cash, split across 10 shares at $50 each. If it spends the $20 buying back and cancelling 0.4 of a share, the company is now worth $480 across 9.6 shares. Your share stays at $50, and you now own a slightly bigger slice of future profits. Many companies prefer buybacks because they're easy to pause in a slow year, whereas cutting a dividend usually panics investors.

## No dividend is guaranteed

A company does not owe you a dividend the way a borrower owes interest on a loan. If business turns sour, management can cut or cancel the payout overnight, so buying a stock just because it currently pays a big dividend can easily backfire.

In the end, a dividend is simply one way a profitable business shares its cash with its owners. Whether a company pays those profits out or keeps them working inside the business, what builds wealth over decades is keeping the money invested so it can keep compounding.

title: Value vs growth stocks
summary: How investors judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive on profits and book value, why value beat growth for a century, and why that flipped after 2007.
youtubeTitle: Value vs growth stocks
body:
You have $100 to invest, and you are choosing between a steady supermarket chain and a fast-growing software firm. Either way you become a part-owner of a real business, so what matters is what your $100 actually buys.

To judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive, investors mostly check two things: how much profit the company makes, and how much it owns.

## Two ways to measure a cheap stock

The first yardstick is profit. Suppose your $100 of supermarket shares buys a slice of $10 a year in profit. You are paying ten years of profit for the business, a **price-to-earnings ratio (P/E)** of 10. That $10 belongs to you as a part-owner whether the supermarket pays it out in cash or puts it back into the business to open new stores or pay down debt.

At the software firm, the same $100 might buy a slice earning just $2 a year, or fifty years of profit (a P/E of 50). At first sight that looks less attractive, unless you expect those profits to grow fast.

The second yardstick is **book value**: add up what a company owns, such as stores, trucks, and cash, and subtract all of its debts. In our example, your $100 of supermarket shares are backed by about $90 of stores and cash. At the software firm, which owns little more than offices and laptops, your $100 is backed by only about $10.

A **value stock** is one that looks cheap on these yardsticks compared to the rest of the market, usually judged on a mix of both, like the supermarket. Index providers such as MSCI and S&P combine measures like price-to-book and price-to-earnings into one score, while Russell relies mainly on price-to-book. A **growth stock** sits at the other end, priced high against its current profits and assets because investors expect fast growth.

## Expectations are baked into the price

Two dollars a year on $100 is a 2 percent return on current earnings, less than even a safe US government bond pays (about 4 percent on a 10-year Treasury). Nobody accepts that unless they expect the software company's profits to multiply.

Because those high hopes are already built into the price, there is little room for a slip. If the software firm keeps growing, just slower than investors hoped, disappointed owners sell and the share price can drop hard. With the supermarket, you already get 10 percent a year on current earnings and nobody expects miracles. If the business holds up better than pessimists feared, buyers step in and push the stock up.

## A century of value winning, then a flip

For most of the last hundred years, buying cheap paid off. In Kenneth French's US stock market dataset, which sorts companies by price against book value, the cheapest third of US stocks returned about 13.2 percent a year from July 1926 to June 2026 (including reinvested dividends). The priciest third returned about 10.2 percent a year.

Three extra percentage points a year sound modest until they compound over a century: $1 invested in the cheapest third grew to about $231,000, while $1 in the priciest third reached about $16,000, roughly fourteen times as much money for value investors. Value beat growth in every decade from the 1940s through the 1980s, and again in the 2000s after the dot-com crash.

From 2007 to 2026, though, the tables flipped. Between January 2007 and September 2026, US growth stocks returned about 13.1 percent a year while value lagged at roughly 9.7 percent. Over those nearly twenty years, $100 grew to about $1,131 in growth stocks and $616 in value, so growth investors ended up with almost twice as much money. Giant tech firms grew their profits fast enough to outrun their steep price tags, while traditional businesses like banks and retailers fell behind.

## Where the yardstick breaks

Part of that slump comes down to the yardstick itself. Accounting rules count physical stores, machines, and cash as assets, while software a company writes itself, research, and brand value are mostly booked as expenses instead of showing up on the balance sheet. As researchers Baruch Lev and Anup Srivastava pointed out in 2019, that can make hugely profitable tech firms look far more expensive on paper than they really are.

The other risk is simpler: sometimes a stock is cheap because the business really is shrinking. Buying a fading company just because its price looks low is what investors call a **value trap**. A low price alone does not make a bargain. Value investing works when an overlooked company beats low expectations, while growth investing works when a fast business keeps clearing a much higher bar.

title: How Paul Volcker pushed interest rates to 20 percent
summary: In 1982 Paul Volcker faced 3,000 home builders he was putting out of business, after letting borrowing costs hit 20% to stop prices rising 12% a year.
youtubeTitle: How Volcker pushed interest rates to 20%
body:
In January 1982, three thousand home builders packed a hotel hall in Las Vegas to hear from the one man who was putting them out of business. His name was Paul Volcker, he was the head of America's central bank, and he was doing it on purpose. He had also given in once before, so the question in that hall was whether he would give in again.

## When borrowed money was free

It had started with prices. In 1979 they were rising almost 12 percent a year, while a 30-year house loan cost about 11 percent. That made borrowed money practically free, because whatever you bought with it went up in price faster than the loan cost you. So people did the obvious thing. They borrowed, and they bought the house and the car this year, before the price went up again, and all that buying pushed prices up even further.

## Going after the cheap money

That summer President Carter handed the problem to Volcker, a man of six foot seven with a cheap cigar, who took a pay cut of almost half to do the job. Volcker went after the cheap money. If a loan gets expensive enough, you don't buy the house, and once enough people stop buying, prices stop climbing.

But when people stop buying houses and cars, the people who build them lose their jobs. By the spring of 1980 that was happening, and Volcker backed off. Borrowing got cheap again, and by July prices were rising 13 percent a year, faster than on the day he started.

## Twenty percent

So he started over, and this time he let the cost of borrowing go all the way to 20 percent. In December 1980 the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans reached 20 percent for the first time. Nobody felt that like the builders. On an ordinary $60,000 house loan over 30 years, the monthly payment was about $580 at 11 percent, and at the 17 percent of 1981 it was about $850. Families stopped buying, and builders who had been in business for decades went bankrupt. Herman Smith, a builder from Fort Worth and the head of their association, said small businesses simply could not survive this, and builders mailed Volcker pieces of two-by-four with "lower interest rates" written on them.

Then it got worse than mail. On 7 December 1981 a man walked into the central bank's building in Washington with a shotgun, and he got as far as the floor where the board was meeting before a guard caught him. Police said he had wanted to take the board hostage because of the interest rates.

## The speech in Las Vegas

Seven weeks later Volcker stood up in front of the builders. They had just had their worst year in decades, with fewer new homes started in 1981 than in any year since at least 1959. They had seen him back off once, and they had every reason to think that enough pressure would work a second time. He told them he knew how bad it was for them, and then he said: "I am convinced we cannot let up now." If he stopped, everything they had been through would have been for nothing, and it would only come back worse later. "I know of no quick fix." A reporter from Time magazine wrote that the mood in the room was distinctly chilly.

## After the speech

He didn't let up. By the summer of 1982 prices were rising about 6 percent a year, and borrowing got cheaper again. The bill came at the same time: by winter more than one American worker in ten had no job.

Volcker later wrote how he knew he had won. His driver, Mr. Pena, had bought a book called *How to Live with Inflation*, and only because it had been marked down from $10.95 to $1.98.

Prices in America have not risen 12 percent a year since. They came closest in 2022, at about 9 percent, and in a Senate hearing that March the head of the central bank, Jerome Powell, was asked whether he was willing to do what Volcker did. He said he hoped history would record that the answer was yes, and the central bank reached for the same cure: the rate on a 30-year house loan went from about 3 percent at the end of 2021 to about 7 percent by October 2022. The cure works the way it did in 1981, by making borrowing expensive until people stop buying, and Volcker's first try in 1980 shows what happens when it stops before prices do.

title: What is market cap?
summary: Market cap is the share price times the number of shares. Why it beats the share price for judging size, and why it is a price, not money.
youtubeTitle: Market cap explained: what a company is \"worth\" and why the share price won't tell you
body:
On 29 October 2025, Nvidia became the first company in history to be worth five trillion dollars. That number is its **market cap**, short for market capitalization, and you can work it out yourself with one multiplication.

A company like Nvidia is cut into small pieces called **shares**, and whoever buys one owns a tiny piece of the company. That day one Nvidia share closed at $207.04, and there were about 24.3 billion of them. Multiply the two and you get $5.03 trillion. That is all a market cap is: the price of one share times the number of shares, which is what the stock market says the whole company is worth.

## Why the share price alone tells you little

Because a market cap has two parts, the share price on its own says very little about how big a company is. Nvidia showed this in June 2024, when it split every share into ten. If you owned one share worth about $1,200 before the split, you owned ten shares at about $120 each after it. You still had your $1,200, and Nvidia was worth just as much as before, because ten times as many shares at a tenth of the price comes out the same.

So a cheap share does not mean a small company, and an expensive share does not mean a big one. You only know how big a company is once you multiply its share price by the number of shares.

## How it steers your index fund

That is why rankings of the most valuable companies go by market cap. It also decides where your money goes in an index fund. A fund that follows the S&P 500 buys the shares of 500 big American companies at once, but it does not split your money evenly. The bigger a company's market cap, the bigger its slice.

If every company got the same, each would get 20 cents of every $100 you put in. In 2025, Nvidia alone made up about 8 percent of the S&P 500, so it got about $8 of your $100, forty times an equal share.

## It is a price, and prices move

A market cap moves whenever the share price moves. In January 2025, a Chinese start-up called DeepSeek showed an AI model that it said was built for a fraction of the usual cost, on less powerful Nvidia chips. Investors feared the world would need fewer of Nvidia's expensive chips, and they sold. On Monday, 27 January, Nvidia's share price fell just under 17 percent, from $142.62 to $118.42, and its market cap dropped by $593 billion. No company on Wall Street had ever lost that much value in one day.

Yet nobody handed over $593 billion. Only about three in every hundred Nvidia shares changed hands that day. The lower price those shares sold at became the price of every share, so everyone who owned Nvidia was suddenly poorer on paper, even if they never sold.

So to see how big a company is, look at its market cap and never at the share price alone. Just remember that a market cap is the last price someone paid, times all the shares, and not money anybody actually has.

title: The VIX, the fear index
summary: The VIX turns what people pay for stock market insurance into one number, the swing they expect over the next month.
youtubeTitle: What is the VIX? The fear index explained, from 1929 to the Covid crash
body:
On the sixteenth of March 2020, as the Covid panic peaked, the American stock market fell twelve percent in a single day, and the VIX, often called the fear index, closed at 82.69. That is still the highest it has ever closed. But 83 what? And how do you put a number on fear in the first place?

## It starts with insurance

Say you have $10,000 in an S&P 500 fund, so your money is spread over five hundred big American companies, and you're nervous about the next month. You can buy a contract that works like insurance: you pay a fee now, and if the market falls, the contract pays you money to make up for it. These contracts are called **options**.

The fee for that insurance isn't fixed. When lots of people get nervous at once, they all want it, and the people selling it ask for more, because the bigger the swings, the more they might have to pay out. Cboe, an options exchange in Chicago, reads these prices backwards all day long. The pricier the insurance, the bigger the swings the market is bracing for over the next month, and the **VIX** is that expected swing, written as one number.

## How to read the number

The VIX is a percentage, and it's written per year, so to read it for the next month you divide it by about three and a half. Since 1990 it has averaged about 20. A VIX of 20 means that in about two months out of three, the S&P 500 should stay within about 6% over the next month, so your $10,000 would stay within about $600, up or down.

At 83, on that day in March 2020, people were bracing for a move of about 24% in a single month. On your $10,000 that's roughly $2,400 either way, about a quarter of your money.

## Why it's called the fear index

When prices keep climbing for years, people call it a bull market, and in those years the VIX sits low, somewhere between 10 and 15. When stocks fall by a fifth or more, people call it a bear market, and then the VIX shoots up, because that's exactly when everybody wants insurance at once. It did after the dot-com bubble burst, reaching 45 in 2002. It got past 80 in the 2008 financial crisis, and in 2020 it went higher still.

## Before the VIX existed

The VIX only goes back to 1990. For the years before, you can still look at how much the market really moved from day to day and put that on the same scale as the VIX. In the fifties and sixties, when stocks mostly climbed, those swings stayed around 10. In the Great Depression after the crash of 1929, the market didn't calm down for a whole decade: all through the thirties the swings averaged about 30, a level the VIX today only reaches in a crisis.

## Its one big weakness

On the nineteenth of February 2020, the S&P 500 closed at a record high, and the VIX was at 14, as calm as in a good year. Five weeks later the market had lost a third of its value, and the fear index only jumped once the fall had already begun. Its record close came on the sixteenth of March, when most of the fall was already behind it.

So the VIX tells you how scared people are today, measured in what they pay for insurance, but it won't tell you when the next shock arrives.

title: What is the risk-free rate?
summary: The risk-free rate is what a short loan to the US government pays. Every other investment has to beat it, so when it jumped in 2022, prices fell.
youtubeTitle: What is the risk-free rate?
body:
If you lend ten thousand dollars to the US government for three months by buying a Treasury bill, you can be practically certain you'll get it back with interest. The government borrows in dollars, and it can always print more of them, so it never runs out. In November 2026 a three-month bill paid about 4.3 percent a year, which on $10,000 comes to about $430. That interest is what's called the risk-free rate, and this one number ends up setting the price of almost everything else.

## The floor under every investment

Anyone can get those $430 without taking any risk, so every other investment gets measured against them. A stock, a company's bond or an apartment you rent out can all lose you money. They're only worth it if they're expected to pay clearly more than the Treasury bill, and the extra you get for taking that risk is what traders call the risk premium.

## When the floor was on the ground

That floor moves, though, and in 2021 Treasury bills paid so little, about 0.05 percent on average, that $10,000 would have earned about five dollars over the whole year. With a floor that low almost anything beat it, so lots of investors saw stocks as the only place worth putting money. There was even a motto for it: TINA, short for "there is no alternative".

Then inflation took off. The Fed raised its rate seven times in 2022, from a range of 0 to 0.25 percent up to 4.25 to 4.5 percent, and Treasury bills followed. By the end of that year a three-month bill paid about 4.4 percent, so the same $10,000 would earn about $440, guaranteed.

## Why a higher safe rate pulls prices down

Say a company expects to earn $100 ten years from now. When the safe rate is zero, those $100 are worth about $100 to you today. At 4.4 percent they're worth only about $65, because $65 in Treasury bills at 4.4 percent a year would grow to $100 by then on their own. The further away a profit lies, the more a higher safe rate shrinks what it's worth today.

That's why tech shares, whose big profits lie furthest in the future, were among the hardest hit in 2022, and the S&P 500 lost about 19 percent that year. Bonds fell too. At the end of 2021 a 10-year Treasury paid about 1.5 percent, and nobody pays full price for an old bond like that when a safe bill pays four, so old bonds lost value and 2022 became one of the worst years for bonds in history.

## What "risk-free" doesn't cover

Risk-free only means you get your dollars back, not what they can buy. In 2021, the year $10,000 in Treasury bills earned about five dollars, consumer prices rose 7 percent, the biggest rise in a year since 1982. To buy the same things at the end of the year you'd have needed $10,700, so the perfectly safe money lost about $700 of buying power.

It's also only risk-free in dollars. If you spend euros or francs, the exchange rate adds a risk of its own, which is why every currency has its own risk-free rate, taken from what its own government pays to borrow.

So the risk-free rate doesn't promise that you come out ahead. It's the bar every other investment has to clear, and when that bar goes up, everything else usually has to get cheaper to clear it again.

title: Book value explained
summary: Book value is what a company owns minus what it owes, according to its own books. It is one piece of the share price, next to profits and expected growth.
youtubeTitle: Book value explained
body:
When you buy a share, you own a small slice of a company, so it's fair to ask what is behind that slice. The company's own accounts give one answer. If it sold everything it owns at the values written in its books and paid off every debt, whatever is left over would belong to the shareholders. That leftover is called its **book value**, because it is the number in the company's accounting books.

## The books of a bike maker

Take a bike maker. For every share, its books list $10 of factory, machines, bikes and cash, and it owes $4 per share to banks and suppliers. So each share is backed by $6 of book value.

Companies on the stock market publish these numbers in their reports. The total usually appears as shareholders' equity, and if you divide it by the number of shares you get the book value behind one share, so you can look it up before you buy.

## What the books record

The values in those books are mostly what things cost. The bike maker's factory sits in its books at what the company paid for it, minus a bit of wear every year. The books don't say what the factory would sell for today.

## What never makes it into the books

Some things never show up in the books at all. Coca-Cola spends billions on advertising every year, about $4.7 billion in the first nine months of 2026 alone, and all of it is counted as costs. The accounting rules only let a company list brands it bought from someone else, never one it built itself. Coca-Cola's books do list brands it bought, like BodyArmor at $2.4 billion, but the Coca-Cola name itself isn't there.

## Book value and the share price

That's why book value on its own doesn't tell you what a share is worth. It goes into the share price next to things like profits and expected growth. The books don't count any profits still to come, so a share usually costs more than its book value.

If people expect the bike maker to keep selling bikes, its share can easily cost more than $6. On 2 October 2026 Coca-Cola's books showed $37.4 billion of equity for its shareholders, about $8.69 a share. In November the share traded at about $96, roughly 11 times its book value. Investors pay that much for the profits its brand keeps bringing in.

## Where book value matters most

Book value matters most for banks and insurers. What they own is mostly money, bonds and other things with a clear market price, so their books come close to what all of it is really worth, and bank shares usually trade around their book value.

So book value tells you what's behind your share on paper, and it's one piece of the share price, next to the profits and growth investors expect.

title: "The bro investor: does a stock hunch beat an index fund?"
summary: A bro puts his $10,000 on one stock he has a hunch about instead of a boring index fund. Here is how that usually turns out, and why.
youtubeTitle: The bro investor: does one stock hunch beat a boring index fund?
body:
The bro investor knows he should be investing, and he has even heard of ETFs. But an ETF only ever gets you what the market does, and he wants big returns, because no risk, no fun. What he has instead is a hunch. Suddenly everyone at his gym drinks the same energy drink, so he puts all his savings, ten thousand dollars, into the company that makes it. Does his hunch beat the boring fund he skipped?

## Why the hunch is already in the price

His hunch might even be right. The trouble is that by the time a drink is in every gym fridge, everybody has noticed. The company's sales show up in its quarterly reports for anyone to read, and the price already counts on the drink taking off. So the crowd, bro included, buys after the jump.

There are so many bros like him by now that together they can move a stock's price, at least a small company's. A study of Robinhood users found that on the days they pile into a stock, it is up about 14 percent on average. Over the following month, those stocks did about 5 percent worse than the market, and the effect showed up only in companies worth less than a billion dollars. So the jump the crowd creates tends to slide back within a month, and the bros who bought on the way up take the loss.

## Twenty-five bros at one gym

Now picture twenty-five bros at his gym, each putting ten thousand dollars on his own hunch. Going by how American stocks have actually done over the years, about one of them catches a giant, a stock that grows huge and makes him rich. About seven more beat the boring fund. The other seventeen end up behind it, and ten of those have less than the ten thousand dollars they put in.

Those counts come from what happened to real stocks. Looking at every company in the Russell 3000 from 1980 to 2014, J.P. Morgan found that two thirds of them did worse than the index over their lifetime, and four in ten lost money outright. Scale that to twenty-five bros and you get seventeen behind the fund and ten in the red.

## A handful of giants

The reason is that the market's gains come from a handful of giants. Hendrik Bessembinder studied ninety years of American stocks, about 26,000 of them from 1926 to 2016, and found that about one company in twenty-five made the stock market's whole gain. All the others together did about as well as a safe loan to the government, the one-month Treasury bills that pay a small interest rate with next to no risk.

A fund that owns the whole market doesn't have to guess which company that will be. It holds all twenty-five hunches at once, giant included, so it gets the giant's gain whichever company it turns out to be. The bro holds one, and most likely it is not the giant.

## The one you hear about

And guess which bro you hear about. It's the one with the giant, telling the whole gym his hunch paid off, while the ten who lost money keep quiet. That makes picking a single stock look a lot better than it is, because the stories that reach you are the winners' stories.

So our bro is most likely not the loud one but one of the seventeen behind the boring fund he skipped, maybe even with less than the ten thousand dollars he put in. And the giant he was hoping his hunch would catch was in the boring fund all along.

title: What is a run rate?
summary: A run rate stretches a few recent weeks of sales to a whole year. Anthropic's $81 billion shows why companies use it and why it is not money made.
youtubeTitle: What are run rates? Anthropic's $81 billion run rate and its problems
body:
In the papers Anthropic filed before going public, it put its run rate at about $81 billion a year. Yet in the whole of 2025, the company behind Claude took in $4.6 billion. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them explains what a run rate is.

## What a run rate measures

A **run rate** takes what a company sold over a short, recent stretch and multiplies it out to a whole year, as if that stretch just kept repeating.
