Anthropic does it in two parts: it takes what customers paid for using Claude over the last 28 days and multiplies that by 13, which covers 52 weeks, and it takes what its subscriptions bring in each month and multiplies that by 12. Add the two together and you get the run rate, about $81 billion as of 31 October 2026.

So a run rate works a bit like a speedometer. It tells you how fast a company is selling right now, and not how much it has actually sold.

## Why companies quote it

If last year's sales are a real, finished number, why not just use that? Because when a company grows this fast, last year's total is out of date before anyone reads it. At $81 billion a year, Anthropic sells about $6.75 billion a month, which is more in a single month than the $4.6 billion it took in during all of 2025. Even its actual revenue for the third quarter of 2026, almost $17 billion, works out to more than $5.6 billion a month. The yearly total would make the company look many times smaller than it is today, and the run rate comes much closer to how big it is right now.

## The month has to repeat

The catch is that a run rate only turns into real money if that month really does keep repeating for a whole year. In 2025, about $3.8 billion of Anthropic's revenue came from customers paying for how much they use Claude, against $789 million from subscriptions. That is more than four out of every five dollars, and if those customers use less next month, they simply pay less.

If a big customer finishes its project, or everyone takes time off over the holidays, the next month comes in smaller and the run rate drops with it. Anthropic's own filing warns that the holidays can swing the number, and it also says the figure is not a forecast and not a substitute for revenue under the usual accounting rules.

## Everyone counts differently

There is no official rule for working out a run rate, so every company counts in its own way, and Anthropic's filing says nobody outside the company has checked its number.

About half of Anthropic's sales in 2025, $2.16 billion or 47 percent, went through Amazon and Google, which sell Claude to their own cloud customers. When a customer pays Amazon $100 for Claude, Amazon keeps roughly $16 of it, yet Anthropic still counts all $100 as its own sales. OpenAI, by contrast, counts only its own cut of what partners like Microsoft bring in. That means you can't simply line up Anthropic's run rate against OpenAI's and say which company is bigger.

## Sales, not what is left

Even a run rate that holds up only counts what customers pay, before the company pays for all the computing power it runs on. In the third quarter of 2026, Anthropic took in almost $17 billion and still made an operating loss of $567 million.

So when you see a run rate in a headline, read it as how fast a company is selling right now, counted the way that company chose, and not as money it has already made.

title: Why wealth taxes failed, and how Zucman would fix them
summary: Most of Europe dropped its wealth taxes because the richest found ways around them. Gabriel Zucman's minimum tax is built to close those holes.
youtubeTitle: Why wealth taxes failed, and Zucman's fix
body:
Most taxes take a cut of what you earn. A **wealth tax** works differently: it takes a small slice of what you own, your home, your savings, your shares, and it takes it every year, whether you earned anything that year or not. In 1990, twelve European countries had one. Today only three still do, Switzerland, Norway and Spain. So what went wrong, and what could we do to fix it?

## Where the old taxes leaked

The old wealth taxes kicked in fairly low. In France the line sat at 1.3 million euros, so the tax didn't only hit the very rich. It also hit families who were rich mostly on paper, for example because the house they had lived in for decades had gone up in value. They owed the tax every year but had little cash to pay it with.

Company owners have the same problem, because their money is tied up in the business and not sitting in a bank account. So from the very start, France left shares in a company you run out of the tax. The trouble is that this is exactly where the biggest fortunes sit. For the few hundred richest households in France, a tax that was 1.5 percent on paper came to about 0.15 percent of their wealth, a tenth of the official rate.

## Zucman's minimum tax

The French economist Gabriel Zucman would turn that around. His tax only starts at 100 million euros, which in France means about 1,800 households, and company shares count like everything else.

He aims at the very top because that is where income tax misses the most. A billionaire's fortune mostly grows inside their companies, and as long as they don't sell their shares, that growth isn't income, so income tax barely touches it. By Zucman's estimate, billionaires pay only about 0.3 percent of their wealth in tax each year.

So his tax is a **minimum**. You add up the taxes you already pay, and if they come to less than 2 percent of your wealth, you pay the difference. Take a fortune of a billion euros: at 0.3 percent its owner pays about 3 million a year, and the minimum brings that up to 20 million. Someone whose taxes already come to 2 percent of their wealth pays nothing extra.

## What if the rich just leave?

The other way to dodge a wealth tax is to move. When Norway raised its wealth tax for 2022, at least thirty of its richest people moved away that year, more than in the thirteen years before put together.

Zucman's tax follows you. In the version France voted on, someone who had lived in France for more than ten years would keep paying it for five years after leaving. A person ready to wait that out could still go, but they would have to move their whole life abroad and would save nothing for five years. So Zucman's bigger fix is getting the big economies to agree on the same minimum, so there's nowhere left to move to. Countries have done this before: in 2021, more than 130 of them agreed on a minimum tax of 15 percent for big companies.

## Where it stands

In Zucman's reading, the old wealth taxes failed because they were full of holes, not because the richest can't be taxed. In France, his version passed the lower house of parliament in February 2025, and polls that year had most of the French behind it. Then the Senate threw it out, and no budget has included it since. So the plan to close the holes is written, but so far it isn't law anywhere.

title: "The South Sea Bubble: how even Isaac Newton got caught"
summary: In 1720 a London company that barely traded saw its shares go from £128 to about £1,000. Isaac Newton sold in time, bought back in, and lost.
youtubeTitle: The South Sea Bubble: how even Isaac Newton got caught
body:
In the summer of 1720, one share of the South Sea Company in London cost about £1,000. A London craftsman earned something like £31 a year, so a single share was more than thirty years of his pay. Back in January the same share had cost £128. The company was supposed to trade with South America, and it never made real money doing that. Yet by the end of that summer Isaac Newton had almost everything he owned in it. So what was the company actually selling?

## A deal with the government

It was selling a deal with the British government. Britain owed a fortune from its wars, and the South Sea Company offered to take most of that debt over. Anyone the government owed money to could hand in that claim and get South Sea shares for it instead.

The company made its money on the swap like this. For every £100 of debt it took over, it was allowed to create one new share. But it handed those shares out at about their market price, not at £100. Say the government owed you £500 and a South Sea share was trading at £500. You got one share. The company had printed five for your debt, so it kept the other four and sold them for cash. The higher the share price went, the more shares were left over and the more the company made, so its real business was its own share price, not trade.

## Pushing the price up

So the company pushed that price up any way it could. The politicians who had to vote for the deal received shares without paying for them, and they gained with every rise in the price. John Aislabie, the finance minister who presented the plan to Parliament, made £200 for every pound the share went up. On 7 April 1720 the deal became law.

One of the directors, John Blunt, had the company lend people money to buy its shares, and new shares could be paid for in instalments. Almost anyone could get in now, and everyone did, from peasants to lords. The price went from £330 in March to £550 by the end of May, and on towards £1,000.

## One week in April

Newton had held South Sea shares for years, and at the start of 1720 they made up almost half of his fortune. That April he decided it would end badly. He sold on Tuesday the 19th, the company's shareholders met on Thursday the 21st, and by Saturday the 23rd he had sold every share, with a profit of about £20,000. The day after that meeting, a bookseller named Thomas Guy started selling his shares too.

But the price kept climbing. In June, Newton sold the government bonds he held and put the money back into South Sea shares. Guy stayed out.

## Nothing underneath

Nothing behind the shares had changed. The government paid the company the same interest whether a share cost £100 or £1,000, so at those prices the only thing holding the share up was the next buyer. In August the next instalments came due, and some people sold shares to pay them. The price began to slide, and Newton kept buying. With no new buyers coming, nothing held it up. By the end of September a share was down to £150, and thousands of people were ruined.

## The score

Parliament went after the people who had run it. Aislabie was thrown out of Parliament and locked in the Tower of London. Blunt had a fortune of close to £200,000 and was left with £5,000. Thomas Guy, who had sold in April and never went back, ended the year five times richer, with a profit of about £175,000, and he used the money to found Guy's Hospital in London, which still carries his name.

Newton had been worth just over £30,000 before the bubble. By the middle of 1721 he was worth about £20,000. He had lost his whole profit and a third of what he started with. In a letter in 1724 he wrote: "I lost very much by the South Sea company which makes my pockets empty." He was still rich, so the line exaggerates, but he had lost a lot. He had seen in April how it would end, and the rising price pulled him back in anyway.

title: "Cutting margins: the Costco story"
summary: Costco adds at most 14% to what it pays and makes its money on the membership card. Wall Street hated it in 2003. Jim Sinegal refused to give in.
youtubeTitle: Cutting margins: the Costco story
body:
At Costco, a hot dog and a soda cost a dollar fifty, just like they did in 1985. Craig Jelinek, who later ran the company, once went to its co-founder Jim Sinegal and told him, "Jim, we can't sell this hot dog for a buck fifty. We are losing our rear ends." Sinegal's answer: "If you raise the effing hot dog, I will kill you. Figure it out."

That was how he ran all of Costco, and Wall Street thought he was throwing money away.

## One rule for every price

Sinegal and a partner opened the first Costco in Seattle in 1983, and he set one rule for every price in it. What a shop adds on top of what it paid for something is its markup. At Costco, the markup on a brand-name product can't be more than 14 percent (15 on its own Kirkland brand), where a supermarket usually adds about 25 percent and a department store 50 or more.

And that 14 percent doesn't leave much. Ian Gordon, an analyst at Bernstein, said it basically just covers the cost of doing business, which means running the warehouses and paying the staff.

## The money is in the card

So where does Costco make its money? Before you can buy anything there, you pay $65 a year for a membership. In its 2025 financial year Costco took in about $5.3 billion in membership fees, against an operating profit of about $10.4 billion, so the card brings in about half of everything Costco earns.

That only works if people pay again next year, and they only do that if the prices inside make the card worth it. So every price Sinegal refused to raise is part of what brought members back.

He kept prices low even where nobody would have noticed. Costco sold so many of one kind of shirt that it got a better price from the maker, and the shirt went from $17.99 down to $12.99. Sinegal could have charged more, and he knew it: "Who the hell's going to notice if you charge $14.99? Well, we're going to know."

## Wall Street's verdict

To Wall Street, that was money that could have gone to the shareholders. An analyst at Deutsche Bank summed it up: "At Costco, it's better to be an employee or a customer than a shareholder."

On 5 August 2003, Costco warned that its profits would be lower than expected. Investors who were already fed up with all that generosity sold, and the share price fell 19 percent in a single day. Afterwards, Costco's finance chief took Sinegal around to meet investors, and as Gordon remembers it, he got beaten up a little.

What they wanted was simple: raise some prices. Sinegal refused and said that doing so would be Costco's downfall. "Those people are in the business of making money between now and next Tuesday," he said about Wall Street. "We're trying to build an organization that's going to be here 50 years from now."

## Who was right

The prices stayed low, and people kept renewing their card: more than nine out of ten members in the US and Canada do. Costco's shares are now worth more than thirty times what they were on that day in August 2003, so whoever sold in the panic missed all of it.

The money Sinegal refused to take on hot dogs and shirts came back to Costco anyway, as more than five billion dollars a year from people paying just to walk in.

title: What is a cap table?
summary: A cap table lists who owns how many shares of a company. Why every funding round shrinks everyone's percent, and when that is still good news.
youtubeTitle: The cap table explained: why a founder's slice shrinks every time a startup raises money
body:
When Facebook got started in 2004, it belonged to three college students. Mark Zuckerberg held about two thirds of the shares, and his two friends held the rest. A list like that, with every owner, how many shares they hold and what percent of the company that makes, is called a **cap table**, short for capitalization table. If you ever work at a startup that pays you partly in shares, your name ends up on such a list too.

A young company needs money, though, and all it can really offer in return is a piece of itself.

## New shares, smaller slices

The first outside money came in August 2004, when Peter Thiel put in $500,000 for about a tenth of Facebook. To give him that tenth, the company made brand-new shares. Zuckerberg kept every share he had, but now there were more shares in total, so his slice of the company was smaller.

This shrinking is called **dilution**. It hits everyone already on the list each time the company raises money, because new money almost always means new shares.

## A smaller slice of a bigger pie

So why would anyone agree to own less? Because the price Thiel paid also put a price tag on the whole company. Half a million dollars for a tenth means all of Facebook was worth about $5 million, and that number is the company's **valuation**.

The money helped Facebook grow. Less than a year later, in May 2005, the venture firm Accel came in at a valuation of $87.5 million. Zuckerberg now owned a smaller slice, but of a much bigger pie, and his shares were worth far more than when Thiel bought in.

## When it goes the wrong way

That only works while each new investor pays more for a share than the one before. If a company runs into trouble, the next investor may only offer a lower price. The same money then buys them a bigger slice, so the company has to make even more new shares to hand it over.

Investors call that a **down round**, and it squeezes everyone already on the list twice. Their slice shrinks further, and this time it is worth less, not more.

## Where Zuckerberg ended up

Facebook kept raising money and handing shares to its employees. When it went public in 2012 at $38 a share, valuing the company at $104 billion, Zuckerberg held about 22 percent of the shares, roughly a fifth. That is a lot. Across 104 tech companies, founders held a median of 15 percent when their company went public. His fifth was worth about $20 billion.

That's the deal on a cap table, yours too if you ever get shares. Your percentage goes down each time the company raises money, and whether that is good news depends on one thing: whether each new investor pays more for a share than the last one did.

title: What is the Dow Jones, and is it useful?
summary: The Dow Jones adds up the share prices of 30 big American companies. Here is who picks them, what that does, and why the S&P 500 makes more sense.
youtubeTitle: The Dow Jones explained: what it is, who picks it, and why the S&P 500 makes more sense
body:
When the news says how the stock market did today, one number you'll almost always hear is the Dow Jones. So what is it actually, and what is it good for?

The Dow is what's called a **stock index**: thirty big companies, all of them American, rolled into one number. Charles Dow, a founder of the Wall Street Journal, started it in 1896 with twelve companies. Back then everything had to be worked out by hand, so he simply added up the price of one share of each company and divided by twelve. A share is one small slice of a company. The Dow is still added up the same way today, only with thirty companies instead of twelve.

## Who picks the thirty

The list isn't fixed. Five people decide who is in: three from S&P Dow Jones Indices, the company that runs the index, and two from the Wall Street Journal. There is no set formula. They look for big, respected companies that keep growing and that lots of investors care about.

When they swap a company, the index has a problem. In June 2026 they replaced the phone company Verizon with Alphabet, Google's parent, and Alphabet's share costs far more than Verizon's did. Since the Dow is a sum of share prices, that swap on its own would have pushed the sum up, and the Dow with it, even though nothing had happened in the market. So they changed the number the sum gets divided by, called the divisor, and the Dow stayed exactly where it was. That's also why today's sum isn't divided by thirty but by a number that has been adjusted again and again.

## Why the share price is all that counts

Because the Dow just adds up share prices, it is **price-weighted**: a company counts by what one of its shares costs, not by how big the company is.

Take the chip maker Nvidia and the bank Goldman Sachs. Nvidia is worth about fourteen times as much as Goldman. But Nvidia is cut into far more slices, so one Goldman share costs almost six times as much as one Nvidia share: about $848 against $146. When both rise one percent, Goldman's price goes up by about $8.48 and Nvidia's by about $1.46. In the Dow's sum, the far smaller company pushes the index up almost six times as far.

## The S&P 500 does it differently

The S&P 500 takes five hundred big American companies and counts each one by what the whole company is worth. You can see the difference on a single day. On 17 April 2025, the health insurer UnitedHealth had the most expensive share in the Dow, so it counted more than any other company there. After a bad profit report, it lost more than a fifth of its price in one day.

In the S&P 500, UnitedHealth was just one of five hundred and barely counted, and since the rest of the market edged up that day, the S&P 500 ended a little higher. The Dow fell more than one percent, all because of that one expensive share.

## So what is the Dow good for?

Days like that are rare. Big companies tend to rise and fall together, so on most days the Dow moves much like the S&P 500. That makes it a fine quick headline, and its history goes all the way back to 1896.

To judge the market, or your own money, the S&P 500 makes more sense, because it counts each company by what it is actually worth rather than by what one of its shares happens to cost. That's also the index people put their money into: the funds that simply buy all of its companies hold more than ten trillion dollars, over a hundred times as much as the funds that copy the Dow.

title: How the gains on a put option change as the stock falls
summary: A put with a $100 strike on a $200 stock gains very little at first, then faster and faster as the stock nears $100, but only if the fall comes in time.
youtubeTitle: A $100 put on a $200 stock: how do the gains change?
body:
Say you have bought a put option with a strike of $100 on a stock that trades at $200. The put runs for a year, and with the stock's implied volatility at 40 percent it costs about $1. The question is how your gain grows as the stock falls toward $100. The short answer is that it does not grow in a straight line.

## The effect of the drop

Ignore time for a moment and look only at the price move. If the stock falls to $150, the put is worth about $4, so the first $50 of the fall has made you about $3. If the stock keeps falling to $100, the put is worth about $16. The second $50 has made you about $12, which is four times as much as the first $50. The same distance in the stock produces a much bigger move in the put.

## Delta and gamma

A put only pays for how far the stock ends up below $100 at the end of the year. At $200 the stock would have to lose more than half its value for that, which is not very likely, so the put barely reacts. A dollar drop in the stock moves the put by only about 3 cents. Traders call that per-dollar number the delta.

As the stock nears $100, the chance that it finishes below the strike goes up, and the delta grows with it. At $100 the delta is about 40 cents, and further down it heads toward a full dollar. How fast the delta grows is called gamma. Gamma is the reason the curve bends upward, and it is largest when the stock is near the strike.

## Time changes the curve

All of this assumed the fall happens right away. A put also loses value as time passes, because there is less and less time left for the stock to fall. With six months left and the stock at $100, the put is worth about $11 instead of $16. If the stock only reaches $100 on the very last day, the put is worth nothing at that point, even though the stock has halved.

So near expiry the curve turns into a sharp corner. The put is worth zero above $100, and below $100 it gains a dollar for every dollar the stock falls.

## A real case

Universa, a fund in Miami, runs a strategy built on this kind of put. It buys out-of-the-money puts at low prices while markets are calm, and waits. In early 2020 the S&P 500 fell by about a third in just five weeks, and implied volatility shot up, which made the puts worth even more on top of that. In March, Universa estimated in a letter to its investors that the strategy had returned about 3,600 percent on the money in it.

## What to take away

The gains on a put do not come in a straight line. They are almost nothing at first and grow faster and faster as the stock nears the strike. But that only pays if the fall comes in time, because a put is a bet with an expiry date.

title: What if a trillionaire's stock halves?
summary: Can one falling stock drag a fortune and other stocks into a spiral? Only if someone borrowed against it. Musk, SpaceX and a 2008 margin call show why.
youtubeTitle: What if a trillionaire's stock halves? How a stock spiral works
body:
Let's say Elon Musk is a trillionaire, and then SpaceX halves. Does that drag other stocks down with it and set off a spiral?

SpaceX very nearly did halve. It went public in June 2026 at $135 a share, and soon after it traded above $225, which pushed Musk's fortune past a trillion dollars. By late July it had fallen to $116.41, almost half below that high, and he was no longer a trillionaire.

## A falling price forces nobody to sell

Musk lost hundreds of billions of dollars in those weeks, and yet nobody handed those billions to anyone. Most of his fortune is his stake in SpaceX, and that stake is valued at the last price someone paid for a share. When the price drops, he is poorer on paper. But the price alone forces nobody to sell anything, and a spiral needs sellers who have no choice.

## Who has no choice

The people with no choice are the ones who borrowed against their shares. Say you put up your shares with a bank as security for a loan. While the shares are worth much more than the loan, the bank is relaxed. When the price falls, the shares stop covering the loan, so the bank asks you for more money, which is called a **margin call**. If you can't pay, the bank can sell your shares without asking you first.

That is where the spiral starts. Dumping a big block of shares pushes the price down further, so the shares you still have cover even less of the loan, the next call comes, and the bank sells again.

## A real spiral: Chesapeake in 2008

Aubrey McClendon co-founded and ran the natural gas company Chesapeake Energy, and he had borrowed against his own shares. When Chesapeake's stock crashed during the financial crisis of 2008, he couldn't meet the calls. Over three days in October, 94 percent of his 31.5 million shares were sold off in a fire sale, for around $600 million. That selling alone pushed the already battered stock down about another 40 percent, and McClendon was left with almost none of his stake.

## Why it didn't happen to Musk

So why didn't the same thing happen to Musk in July? SpaceX's filing before it went public showed that, as of 1 May 2026, only about 238,000 of his 849.5 million SpaceX shares were pledged as security for loans. That is fewer than one in three thousand, so there was almost nothing for a bank to sell. And Tesla's board won't let him borrow more than $3.5 billion against his Tesla shares, which is tiny next to a fortune of around $845 billion. Nobody could force him to sell, so the drop never turned into a spiral.

## How it still reaches other stocks

Even so, a SpaceX drop reaches Tesla. Both stocks are tied to the same man, and in early November 2026 both dropped hard on the same two days. And when Musk wants cash, he sells Tesla. In 2022 he sold about $23 billion of Tesla stock to pay for Twitter, and that, on top of worries about the economy, helped push Tesla down 65 percent that year.

Someone who is forced to sell does the same thing: they sell whatever they can, not just the stock that fell. That is how a spiral can jump from one stock to the next.

## So does it spiral?

If SpaceX halves, Musk loses hundreds of billions on paper, and Tesla can get pulled down with it, but nobody is forced to sell, so it doesn't spiral. A fall only becomes a spiral when the shares were borrowed against, because then it is the bank that decides when they have to be sold.

title: What happens to options when a company is taken private
summary: When a company is bought out for cash, every option on it turns into a fixed sum or nothing. The Electronic Arts deal shows how, step by step.
youtubeTitle: What happens to your calls and puts when a company is taken private
body:
In September 2025, the video game maker Electronic Arts agreed to be taken private. A group of investors around Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, together with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners, offered $210 in cash for every share. A few days earlier, on 25 September, the stock had closed at $168.32, so the offer was about 25 percent above it, and at $55 billion it was the largest all-cash take-private on record. Once a deal like that closes, the stock stops trading and disappears from the market. So what happens to an option on a stock that is about to stop existing?

## The announcement does most of the repricing

Most of the price change happens on the day of the announcement. Within a few days EA traded slightly above $200. If you held a call with a strike of $180, it was suddenly deep in the money and worth about $20 a share.

The other side looked very different. A put with a strike of $190, bought as insurance against a fall, lost most of its value, because the stock had just moved away from it and now had a price waiting at the end. A call with a strike above $210 was in an even worse spot: it only paid if somebody offered more than $210, and nobody expected that.

And with the price pinned like that, implied volatility dropped. The stock had almost no reason to move anymore, and the only big move still possible was the deal falling apart.

## Why the stock stays below the offer

You might expect the stock to jump straight to $210. It didn't, because the buyers only pay once the deal closes, and until then it can still fail. The deal needed sign-offs from shareholders and regulators. The money came from a foreign sovereign wealth fund, so CFIUS, the US committee that reviews foreign investments for national security, had to look at it. And about $20 billion of the $55 billion was borrowed from JPMorgan.

So for months the stock stayed roughly $10 short of the offer: slightly above $200 in early October 2025, and $201.57 in early May 2026. For the stock that gap is small, but for your $180 call it is the difference between $20 and $30 a share, so holding the call had become a bet that the deal would close.

The put at $190 was the opposite bet. If the deal had collapsed, EA would most likely have fallen back toward the $168 where it traded before the news, and the put would have been worth about $22 again.

## What the clearing house does at the closing

The deal did go through. On 4 August 2026 it closed, and every EA share turned into $210 in cash, but the options didn't vanish with the stock.

The Options Clearing Corporation, the clearing house behind every listed option in the US, rewrites each contract in a cash takeover. Instead of 100 shares, a contract now delivers a fixed amount of cash, 100 times the deal price, which for EA is $21,000. Since nothing can move that amount anymore, an option is worth only what it pays at the deal price, with no time value left. Your $180 call is worth exactly $30 a share, or $3,000 a contract, however long it still had to run.

Because there is nothing left to wait for, trading in the options stops and the expiry is pulled forward to shortly after the closing. When Dayforce was taken private for $70 a share in February 2026, the deal closed on 4 February and every Dayforce option, whatever its original date, was moved to expire on 20 February. Anything in the money by at least a cent is exercised automatically. The put at $190 and every call above $210 expire worthless.

## The rule for any cash take-private

When a company is taken private for cash, your options stop being bets on the stock and become a fixed sum:

- a call gets the deal price minus its strike,
- a put gets its strike minus the deal price,
- and if that comes out below zero, you get nothing.

The day the deal is announced, the stock jumps close to the offer and the options are repriced around it. From then until the closing, what is left to bet on is mostly whether the deal goes through.

title: Why a steady company trades at a P/E of 10 to 15
summary: Flip a P/E and you get the earnings yield. Next to a safe bond, it explains why steady companies sit at a P/E of 10 to 15, and why rates move every P/E.
youtubeTitle: Why a steady company trades at a P/E of 10 to 15
body:
A share of JPMorgan, the biggest bank in America, costs about fourteen times the profit the bank makes per share in a year, so its P/E is about 14. Big, steady companies like that usually trade at a P/E somewhere between 10 and 15. So why there, and not at 5, or at 30?

## Turn the P/E upside down

The P/E is the share price divided by the yearly profit per share. Turn it upside down and it tells you something more useful. Say you put $100 into a company at a P/E of 10. Then your shares stand for $10 of the company's profit every year, and as an owner that profit is yours, whether the company pays it out or puts it back into the business.

So the profit behind your shares is 10 percent a year of what you paid. That flipped number is called the **earnings yield**. At a P/E of 5, the same $100 would stand for $20 of profit a year, so 20 percent.

## Compared to what?

Twenty percent sounds amazing, but it only means something next to what else you could do with the money. A ten-year US government bond pays about 5 percent a year right now, and you are almost guaranteed to get your money back.

So if shares of a steady bank really came with 20 percent a year in profit, people would sell their bonds and buy the bank. All that buying pushes its price up until the P/E is closer to 10.

The price settles where the profit comes to what the bond pays plus a couple of points, because a bank can have a terrible year and the government pays no matter what. With the bond at 5 percent, that is around 7 to 10 percent a year, a P/E of about 10 to 15. JPMorgan, at a P/E of about 14, comes to about 7 percent, two points more than the bond.

## The catch: growth

Meta trades at a P/E of about 20, so its profit comes to about 5 percent a year of what you pay. That is no more than the bond pays without any risk. People buy it anyway, because Meta is still growing: the $5 of profit behind your $100 today could be $10 in a few years.

So the logic only holds for a company whose profit stays about the same. A P/E much above 15 is a bet that the profits will grow.

## When the bond rate moves

Because the bond is the yardstick, every P/E moves when its rate moves.

In 2020 and 2021 a ten-year US government bond paid only about 1 percent a year. Next to that, even 5 percent a year from a stock's profits looked like a great deal, and people bought. By the end of 2021 the S&P 500, full of growing tech companies, traded at about 21 times the profits expected for the next year.

Then in 2022 the bond rate climbed to around 4 percent. A stock whose profit came to under 5 percent was suddenly not much better than a safe bond, so people sold. By the end of that year the S&P 500's P/E was down to about 17, and the index had lost about a fifth of its value, while the profits expected for the next year had hardly changed. The fall came almost entirely from a lower price for each dollar of profit.

So a P/E is never high or low on its own. Flip it, and hold it next to what a safe bond pays at the time.

title: What happens when a company is taken private? The Twitter buyout
summary: When Elon Musk took Twitter private in 2022, shareholders got cash, the company got $13 billion of debt, and its numbers disappeared from view.
youtubeTitle: What happens when a company is taken private? Twitter, Musk and the $44 billion deal
body:
In April 2022, Elon Musk offered to buy Twitter, the app that is now called X. Not just a piece of it, either: he offered to buy every single share, at $54.20 each, about $44 billion in all, and in his offer he wrote that Twitter "needs to be transformed as a private company."

Taking a company private means exactly that: one buyer ends up owning all of it, and its shares disappear from the stock exchange. The hard part is getting every owner to sell. On the last trading day before anyone knew Musk was buying, a Twitter share had cost about $39.31, so his offer was about 38 percent higher. That gap is how a buyer gets every owner to sell at once. You offer them far more than the market pays.

## Who pays for the buyout

Twitter's board said yes, and banks lent $13 billion of the price. That loan went onto Twitter itself, with no personal guarantee from Musk, so it was the company that would have to pay it back. Buyers often do it this way, because then the business they buy carries the debt, not them.

For Twitter that was a heavy load. It had lost money in most years of its existence, and now it owed about one and a half billion dollars of interest every year on top of everything else.

## The buyer who wanted out

Then tech stocks fell hard. In July 2022 Musk said he was walking away from the deal, in a fight over how many of Twitter's accounts were fake. Twitter's shares dropped to about $33, because investors doubted the deal would ever close and the $54.20 began to look like a promise that might never be paid.

Twitter sued him to hold him to the deal he had signed. If Twitter won, Musk would have to pay $44 billion for a company the market now priced far lower. In October he gave in and agreed to pay the full price by Friday the 28th, the judge's deadline.

On the Wednesday before, he walked into Twitter's headquarters carrying a bathroom sink and posted "let that sink in." On Thursday the deal closed, and that same day he fired the chief executive and other top managers.

## What happened to the shareholders

The shareholders had voted for the deal in September, and that vote bound all of them. If you owned Twitter shares, it no longer mattered whether you personally wanted to sell. You got $54.20 in cash for every share, and the next morning the stock exchange stopped trading them.

## Answering to nobody

From then on Musk answered to nobody. A private company has no crowd of shareholders who can vote its boss out, and it doesn't have to publish its results every three months. Eight days after the deal closed, Musk started cutting about half the staff. By the next spring, he said, about 1,500 people were left out of just under 8,000, and in the summer of 2023 he renamed Twitter X.

From the outside, nobody could tell how the business was doing. Fidelity, a fund company that owns a piece of X, valued that piece at almost 80 percent less than it had paid. Then in 2025 Musk merged X into his own AI company, xAI, and set X's price himself: $45 billion counting the debt, about what he had paid. That left two very different prices for the same company, and nobody outside could check either of them.

## Back on the stock market

That changed in 2026, when SpaceX bought xAI, with X inside it, and then went public. A company on the stock market has to show its numbers, and they showed that X's advertising brought in $1.8 billion in 2025, less than half of what Twitter made from ads in 2022.

So the shareholders who were bought out got their $54.20 in cash, and most of the staff lost their jobs. That is what taking a company private does: the shareholders take the cash, the company takes the debt, and how it is really doing stays the owner's secret until it comes back to the stock market.

title: What is the Nasdaq?
summary: The Nasdaq is a stock exchange where the tech giants trade, and an index of its companies that swings harder than the market as a whole.
youtubeTitle: What is the Nasdaq? The stock exchange of big tech, and why its index swings so hard
body:
The Nasdaq is one name for two things. It's a stock exchange, and it's also a number that follows the companies traded on that exchange. That number swings a lot harder than the rest of the stock market, and the reason starts with the exchange itself.

## The exchange

A company can be cut into small pieces called shares, and a **stock exchange** is the marketplace where those shares get bought and sold. The best-known one is the New York Stock Exchange, which goes back to 1792, and for most of its history its traders met in person on a trading floor.

The Nasdaq opened on 8 February 1971 as the first stock market with no trading floor at all. It was just computers, matching people who want to buy a share with people who want to sell one.

## Why the tech companies ended up there

For decades the much older New York Stock Exchange didn't let small, new companies list their shares, and the Nasdaq did. It was also far cheaper for a company to be listed on the Nasdaq. So the young tech companies of the seventies and eighties went there instead. Intel was one of the first big companies on the Nasdaq. Apple's shares started trading there in December 1980, and Microsoft's in March 1986.

As those companies grew into giants, they stayed. Today Amazon, Google and Nvidia are traded on the Nasdaq too.

## The index

For you as a buyer, it hardly matters where a share is traded. You tap buy in your app, and the app sorts out the rest. What matters is the second meaning of the name: an **index** called the Nasdaq Composite.

An index is one number that follows the prices of a whole group of companies at once. The Nasdaq Composite follows almost all of the companies on the Nasdaq, which is thousands of them. They don't all count the same, though. A company worth a hundred times more counts a hundred times more. So the tech giants move the number most, and when the Nasdaq falls two percent in a day, it mostly means that big tech had a bad day.

## Why it swings so hard

When the mood about tech turns, the whole index turns with it. In the late nineties investors bought almost anything that had to do with the internet. In March 2000 they started to see that many of those companies were running out of money, and they sold. Since the Nasdaq was full of tech companies, the index fell with them.

On 10 March 2000 the Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 5,048.62. Two and a half years later, on 9 October 2002, it closed at 1,114.11, a fall of 78 percent. If you had put in $1,000 at the very top, you'd have had about $220 left. Over the same stretch the S&P 500, an index of 500 big American companies of every kind, lost about half. The Nasdaq needed fifteen years to get back to its old high, which it finally closed above on 23 April 2015.

It works the other way round too. In 2023 a handful of tech giants, among them Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia, soared. That year the Nasdaq gained 43 percent and the S&P 500 gained 24.

So the Nasdaq mostly tells you how big tech is doing, and tech is the part of the market that climbs faster and falls harder than the rest.

title: Supply and demand, and where it breaks down
summary: How the supply and demand graph sets a price, and the three assumptions real markets often break, from oil and eggs to Bitcoin and wages.
youtubeTitle: Supply and demand, and where it breaks down
body:
Supply and demand is the basic model in economics for how a price gets set. Price sits on the vertical axis, and the amount of something bought and sold sits along the bottom.

Two lines meet on that graph. The **demand** line slopes down, because the cheaper something gets, the more people want to buy it. The **supply** line slopes up, because the higher the price, the more sellers want to make and bring to market.

## Equilibrium, and why prices get pulled there

Where the two lines cross is called the **equilibrium**. It is the one price where the amount people want to buy is the exact amount sellers want to sell.

In the model, a market gets pulled to that crossing point on its own. If the price sits too high, sellers are left with stock nobody buys, so they cut their prices to clear it. If the price sits too low, shelves run empty, and sellers realize they can charge more. Either way, the price moves back toward the cross.

## When supply shifts

The same graph explains why a price changes when something hits the sellers. Fewer sellers, or lower output, means there is less available at every price. The whole supply line moves to the left, and the crossing point moves up to a higher price.

Eggs showed this clearly when bird flu forced farmers to kill more than thirty million egg-laying hens. With far fewer eggs at every price, a dozen eggs in March 2025 hit a record of more than six dollars.

In theory, once supply recovers, the line moves back to the right and the price follows it down. In practice, prices often come down much more slowly than they went up, because sellers can hold them up for a while.

## Where the model breaks down

Every part of the supply and demand graph rests on an assumption, and real markets break them all the time.

### Few sellers

The supply line assumes there are lots of small sellers, none of them big enough to set the price on their own. When there is only one seller, or a small group working together, they can simply decide how much to sell and set the price that way.

In 1973, a group of Arab oil countries cut production and stopped selling oil to the United States. A barrel of oil jumped from about three dollars to nearly twelve.

### Buyers who want more when prices rise

The demand line assumes people buy less as the price goes up. That fails for some luxury goods, like an expensive car, where the high price is part of the point and can attract more buyers rather than fewer.

It also fails in bubbles. With stocks, houses, or Bitcoin, people often buy precisely because the price is already rising, which pushes the price up even further. Bitcoin climbed from about a thousand dollars to almost twenty thousand in 2017, and a year later it was back below three thousand three hundred.

### Prices that barely move

The crossing point assumes prices move freely and quickly. Some prices do not, and wages, the price of work, are the clearest example.

When companies need fewer workers, the graph says wages should fall until everyone who wants a job has one. People do not accept pay cuts easily, so wages can stay above that level, and instead of lower pay for everyone, some people end up without a job.

Supply and demand is still a good first sketch of which way a price should move. It just only holds when there are many sellers, when higher prices put buyers off, and when prices are free to adjust, and in plenty of real markets at least one of those conditions is missing.

title: How inflation and interest rates are tied together
summary: When prices rise fast, interest rates rise with them. Higher rates then cool borrowing and spending, slowing inflation back down.
youtubeTitle: How inflation and interest rates are tied together
body:
**Inflation** is how fast prices rise over a year. An **interest rate** is the yearly price of a loan: what you pay to borrow money, or what you earn for lending it out. The two pull on each other in opposite directions. When prices rise fast, interest rates go up, and those higher rates then slow prices down again.

## Why rising prices push rates up

Say you have $100 today and two choices for the next year. If you keep it in cash and prices rise 8% over the year, the same basket of goods that cost $100 now costs $108, so your cash buys about 8% less than it used to.

Your other option is to lend the $100 out. If the loan pays 5% interest, you get $105 back a year later. That looks like a gain on paper, yet $105 still buys less than your original $100 did when prices rose 8%. Once you subtract inflation from the interest rate, what is left is the real return, and at 5% interest against 8% inflation you end up nearly 3% behind in what your money can actually buy.

To make lending worth doing, the rate has to beat what prices are expected to do. So whenever people expect prices to climb faster, the interest rate lenders ask for climbs with it. That is the first direction of the link: inflation pushes interest rates up.

## Why higher rates slow prices down

On the other side of every loan sits a borrower. When interest rates go up, a mortgage, a car loan, or a company's loan for a new factory all cost more every month. Higher monthly payments nudge households and businesses to borrow less and buy less.

With fewer buyers around, shops and companies can't raise their prices as easily without losing customers. Prices don't suddenly start falling, they just keep rising at a slower pace. That is why a central bank raises its interest rate on purpose when inflation runs too hot. In the United States that is the Federal Reserve, and when the Fed raises its benchmark rate, commercial banks pass the higher cost on to their own loans.

## America from 2022 to 2024

You could watch both halves of that link play out in the US between 2022 and 2024. By June 2022, consumer prices were rising 9.1% over the previous year, while the Fed's target rate was still sitting at 1.5% to 1.75%, far behind inflation.

So the Fed raised its rate again and again, taking it to between 5.25% and 5.5% by July 2023. Borrowing costs jumped across the economy. The average 30-year mortgage rate went from 3.11% at the end of 2021 to 7.08% in October 2022. On a $300,000 mortgage, that took the monthly payment from $1,283 to $2,012, about $730 more every month, and home buying dropped sharply.

## Why it works like a slow brake

Higher interest rates do not cool inflation overnight. A company that is already halfway through building a new factory will often finish it anyway rather than walk away midstream, so higher borrowing costs filter through the economy slowly. Federal Reserve research puts the typical lag at 18 months to two years or more before tighter rates really bite.

By June 2024, two years after US inflation peaked, yearly price growth was back near 3%, with cheaper energy helping bring the overall rate down as well. That is the whole link: when prices rise fast, interest rates move up with them, and those higher rates act as a slow brake that brings prices back under control.

title: What does 100% implied volatility actually mean?
summary: At 100% implied volatility, a symmetric bell curve breaks below zero. Because stock moves multiply, options models use a log-normal curve instead.
youtubeTitle: What does 100% implied volatility actually mean?
body:
If a stock trades at $100 and its options show 100% implied volatility, it is natural to ask whether that implies bankruptcy. Implied volatility is normally read as the typical swing a stock could make over a year, up or down, and down 100% from $100 is zero.

If you draw the usual symmetric bell curve around $100 with a width of 100%, the middle two-thirds of outcomes run from $0 to $200. Worse, the left tail of that curve spills straight past zero into negative stock prices. Because a stock cannot trade below zero, the options market is not using a normal bell curve on dollar prices at all.

## Why stock moves produce a log-normal curve

The reason comes down to how percentage changes work: stock moves multiply rather than add. If a $100 stock drops 50%, it lands at $50. If it drops 50% again, it lands at $25, not $0. You can keep losing half over and over and get closer to zero without ever crossing it.

On the upside, nothing holds the price back in the same way. A stock can double from $100 to $200, and keep climbing from there with no ceiling.

Options models such as Black-Scholes build that asymmetry straight into the math. Instead of putting the symmetric bell curve on dollar prices, they put it on the compounded percentage moves. When you translate that back into dollars, the curve bunches up against zero on the left and stretches into a long tail on the right. That lopsided shape is a **log-normal distribution**.

## Reading 100% implied volatility in dollars

Take our $100 stock and give it no built-in gain, so its average expected price a year from now stays at $100. Run 100% implied volatility through the log-normal curve, and the numbers look very different from the $0 to $200 range of a symmetric bell.

About one time in six, the stock finishes the year below $22. About one time in six, it finishes above $165. The other two-thirds of the time, it lands somewhere between $22 and $165, well clear of zero.

Even though the average expected outcome is still $100, a few big winners far out in the right tail pull that average up. The middle outcome, the median, sits at only about $61, so nearly seven times out of ten, a stock this volatile finishes the year below where it started.

## Past 100% and daily swings

Because implied volatility is not a cap on losses, nothing stops it from climbing well past 100%. It is also always quoted for a full year, even on an option that expires in a few days.

To see what a yearly figure implies for a single trading day, traders use the rule of 16. A year has about 252 trading days, and the square root of 252 is nearly 16, so dividing annualized volatility by 16 gives a rough daily swing. At 100% implied volatility, that works out to about a 6% move in a day.

That is how stocks in extreme frenzies can quote numbers that look absurd on paper. During the January 2021 short squeeze, GameStop's implied volatility reached roughly 1,000%. On the log-normal scale, options were pricing in the stock losing or gaining more than half its value in a single day.

## Where the model stops working

The multiplying math keeps a stock above zero forever, even if it shrinks to pennies. Real markets are not that tidy. Companies do go bankrupt and wipe shareholders out to zero, and real stocks suffer sudden crashes far more often than a smooth bell curve predicts.

So 100% implied volatility is not a bankruptcy forecast. It measures how wide the market expects the swings to be, while the risk of actual bankruptcy stays outside the curve.

title: What actually moves a stock price?
summary: A stock price is the last trade on the order book, so it follows whoever is trading in the biggest hurry with the most money, mostly professionals.
youtubeTitle: What actually moves a stock price?
body:
When a stock jumps or drops in a single afternoon, it is easy to wonder who is behind it: everyday retail investors, big funds and trading firms, or mega-rich whales holding massive stakes. To see how much power each group really has, it helps to start with how a price is made. A stock price is simply the price of the last trade.

## The order book and urgency

For any listed stock, there is a list of people who want to buy a share, each stating the most they would pay, and a list of people who want to sell, each stating the least they would take. Together, those two lists are called the **order book**. Whenever a buyer and a seller agree on a number, a trade happens and that becomes the new price.

Because of that, prices move whenever one side is in more of a hurry than the other. If lots of owners want out at once, they sell to every buyer offering $100, then take $99 from the next group in line, then $98, and the price slides. Buyers in a rush push it up the same way. What puts people in a hurry is what they expect a company to earn and how they feel about it. Only a small slice of a company's shares changes hands on any day, and that small slice sets the price of every share.

## Who owns stocks and who trades them

Ownership of the US stock market is spread across several large groups. In early 2025, Federal Reserve data showed households and nonprofits held about four in ten dollars of American shares directly, a bucket that stretches from everyday savers to very rich families. Investment funds, where many people's money is pooled together, held about a quarter, foreign investors almost a fifth, and pension funds about a tenth. Most of the money inside those funds and pensions belongs to ordinary people too, though professionals are the ones deciding what to buy and sell.

Holding shares is not the same thing as trading them. According to JPMorgan data from early 2025, trading by small investors has more than doubled since Covid, and it still accounts for only about a quarter of US stock trading. The other three quarters is professionals: fund managers, hedge funds, and trading firms buying and selling all day.

## What mega-rich whales can and cannot do

For individual whales, like billionaires sitting on huge stakes, simply holding shares does not prop a price up. To keep lifting a stock, they would have to keep buying with fresh cash. What they can do is push a single stock down when they sell.

In November 2021, Elon Musk asked on Twitter whether he should sell a tenth of his Tesla shares. Voters said yes. Because that much selling would use up all the buyers waiting at the current price, other investors hurried to sell first. In two days, Tesla lost nearly $175 billion in value.

## Who moves the whole market

March 2020 showed who carries the weight across the entire market. The biggest American companies fell by a third in about a month. As one Bloomberg columnist summed it up, Wall Street pros panicked and sold, while small investors at TD Ameritrade bought more shares than they sold, and prices plunged anyway.

On most days, the big funds and trading firms hold the most power, because a stock price follows whoever is in the biggest hurry with the most money. Whales can shake a single stock when they sell, while small investors do only about a quarter of the trading, so their mood rarely sets the price on its own.

title: "Put before earnings: buy now or wait?"
summary: Options price in the earnings jump beforehand and drop in implied volatility right after, so a put bought early can lose money even when the stock falls.
youtubeTitle: Put before earnings: buy now or wait?
body:
Say you want to buy a put option on a stock, and the company reports its quarterly earnings tomorrow. Buying before the report puts you in place if the stock plunges overnight. Waiting until the morning after means you might miss the move. The catch is that options do not cost the same on both days, and the gap between those two prices often decides whether the trade makes or loses money.

## Why puts cost more before earnings

Ahead of an earnings report, nobody knows how the numbers will look, so the stock could easily jump or drop ten percent or more in a single night. That makes selling options dangerous. The people on the other side of the trade demand extra compensation for taking on that overnight risk, which pushes implied volatility up across every contract that is still alive when the numbers come out.

Take a stock trading at $100 and a one-month put with a $100 strike. On the day before earnings, with implied volatility at 70 percent, that put costs about $8. Buying the contract a few weeks earlier does not get around this either. Any option whose expiration sits past the earnings date already has that overnight swing built into its price, because sellers know the event is coming long before the week of the call.

## What happens after the numbers land

The morning after the report, the big unknown is gone. Even if the market still debates what the numbers mean for the rest of the year, the single binary jump is over, so implied volatility collapses overnight in what traders call an IV crush.

Suppose implied volatility falls from 70 percent back down to a normal 45 percent. If the stock opens right where it closed at $100, that same $8 put drops to about $5 right away. You lose $3 overnight without the stock moving a cent.

Even worse, you can get the direction right and still lose money. If the stock falls 4 percent to $96, the put gains value from the lower share price, but the collapse in implied volatility takes away more than the drop adds. Your contract is only worth about $7, still less than the $8 you paid. In this example, the stock has to fall below $94.74, more than 5 percent, just for the put to break even the next morning.

## Why waiting usually pays off

That overnight drop in option prices is why waiting tends to come out ahead. Option sellers do not just price in the size of the move they expect; they add a safety cushion on top for bearing the risk. Across nearly 29,000 US earnings reports tracked by EarningsWatcher between 2023 and 2026, options priced in an average move of about 9.2 percent while stocks closed an average of 6.3 percent away from their pre-earnings price.

If your view is that the stock will drift lower over the next few weeks rather than blow up tomorrow night, buying before the report means paying for an event you are not even trying to trade. Waiting until the morning after lets the IV crush clear out first, so a fresh one-month at-the-money put costs around $5 instead of $8.

## The two cases for buying before

Buying ahead of earnings only makes sense in two situations.

The first is when you expect a much bigger drop than the market is pricing in. If that $100 stock plunges 20 percent to $80 overnight, the $8 put jumps to about $20, more than doubling your money. Anyone who waited for cheaper options after the report missed the entire drop.

The second is when you already own the shares and want protection through the call. If you hold a stock into earnings, waiting until the morning after to buy a put is like buying fire insurance after the house has burned down. You will overpay for that insurance in quiet quarters, because that is the price of having a floor on the one night the stock gaps down hard.

Buying a put before earnings means paying for one night of chaos. Unless that single night is what you are betting on, or what you need protection from, waiting until after the numbers are out keeps you from paying for risk you never wanted.
